title: 6  Payables and Vendors
text:
6.4 Vendor master review
The vendor master decides who can be paid. A fictitious vendor, or a genuine vendor with someone else’s bank account, turns every later control into a formality. So we start here. First, a summary of what each vendor was paid in the year.

vendor_paid <- payments |>
  summarise(paid = sum(amount), payments = n(), first_paid = min(pay_date),
            largest = max(amount), .by = vendor_id)


6.4.1 New vendors paid at once
A genuine new vendor is usually registered, then waits for an order, a delivery and a bill. A vendor paid within days of registration skipped some of that, or was created for one payment. Let us find vendors registered during the year and the number of days to their first payment.

new_vendors <- vendors |>
  filter(created_on >= as.Date("2024-04-01")) |>
  inner_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(days_to_first = as.numeric(first_paid - created_on)) |>
  arrange(days_to_first)

new_vendors |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, created_on, first_paid, days_to_first, paid)

# A tibble: 9 × 6
  vendor_id vendor_name               created_on first_paid days_to_first   paid
  <chr>     <chr>                     <date>     <date>             <dbl>  <dbl>
1 V234      Vindhya Health Distribut… 2024-08-12 2024-08-17             5 2.07e6
2 V293      Maa Durga Medical Agency  2024-06-20 2024-06-25             5 1.54e5
3 V189      Trinetra Medical Agencies 2024-11-04 2024-11-11             7 3.70e6
4 V144      Jyoti Computer Supplies   2024-04-19 2024-05-26            37 4.95e5
5 V213      Suraj Cement Depot        2024-08-06 2024-09-22            47 5.88e5
6 V225      Gopal Cement Depot        2024-05-17 2024-08-20            95 9.05e5
7 V114      Nilgiri Surgicals         2024-07-29 2024-11-18           112 8.24e4
8 V251      Navin Stationers          2024-04-18 2024-08-12           116 7.34e5
9 V111      Sagar Medical Agencies    2024-06-04 2024-10-10           128 3.39e5


9 vendors registered in the year have been paid. 3 of them were paid within a week. Vindhya Health Distributors was paid 5 days after registration. Its first order was for paracetamol at Keshavnagar in August, a season of fevers, and it may well have been an urgent purchase. The file will say. Maa Durga Medical Agency was paid 5 days after registration. We meet it again under duplicate vendors. Trinetra Medical Agencies was paid 7 days after registration, and ₹37 lakh in all, by 20 February 2025.
Each test of this section ends by keeping the ids of the flagged vendors in an object whose name starts with f_, for flag. We combine them all in Section 6.8.

f_new <- new_vendors$vendor_id[new_vendors$days_to_first <= 7]


6.4.2 Dormant vendors that wake up
A vendor that has not been paid for years, and is suddenly paid large amounts, needs a look. Its record may have been reused by someone else. Our past_paid table has payments of the three earlier years. A vendor is dormant if it was registered before April 2022 and was paid nothing in 2022-23 or 2023-24.

recent <- past_paid |>
  filter(fy %in% c("2022-23", "2023-24")) |>
  distinct(vendor_id)

dormant <- vendors |>
  filter(created_on < as.Date("2022-04-01")) |>
  anti_join(recent, by = "vendor_id") |>
  inner_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  left_join(summarise(past_paid, last_paid_in = max(fy), .by = vendor_id), by = "vendor_id")

dormant |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, last_paid_in, first_paid, payments, paid)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  vendor_id vendor_name            last_paid_in first_paid payments     paid
  <chr>     <chr>                  <chr>        <date>        <int>    <dbl>
1 V110      Gopal Office Supplies  2021-22      2025-03-17        1   27841.
2 V135      Deep Computer Supplies 2021-22      2024-12-10        1   34598.
3 V170      Gomti Furniture House  2021-22      2025-03-02        2 1609200 


3 dormant vendors were paid this year. 2 of them received one small payment each, ₹27,841 and ₹34,598, which is what a vendor called back for an odd order looks like. Gomti Furniture House is different. Last paid in 2021-22, it received ₹16.1 lakh in 2 payments from 2 March 2025. The size of the return is the signal, not the return itself.

f_dormant <- dormant$vendor_id[dormant$paid > 5e5]


6.4.3 Bank details changed around a payment
A common payables fraud needs no fake vendor at all. Someone changes a genuine vendor’s bank account to one they control, waits for a large payment, and changes it back. The vendor complains later that it was not paid, or never notices. The current vendor master shows nothing wrong. Only the change log does. Let us look at it.

vendor_changes

# A tibble: 11 × 6
   vendor_id field        old_value    new_value    changed_on changed_by
   <chr>     <chr>        <chr>        <chr>        <date>     <chr>     
 1 V159      bank_account 662071804153 502198464016 2024-05-21 DEO02     
 2 V129      bank_account 502110342100 310414194942 2024-05-23 DEO02     
 3 V188      bank_account 502137953269 502122192533 2024-06-13 DEO02     
 4 V237      bank_account 310471968976 662084191305 2024-06-26 DEO03     
 5 V141      bank_account 662034023569 502145635425 2024-10-02 DEO03     
 6 V179      bank_account 662048058749 662084840488 2024-10-24 DEO02     
 7 V247      bank_account 118714090164 310419552025 2024-12-06 DEO02     
 8 V280      bank_account 662014597032 310434503150 2024-12-16 DEO03     
 9 V158      bank_account 662010793239 502183006249 2024-12-18 DEO03     
10 V127      bank_account 662030224077 118766027194 2025-01-17 DEO04     
11 V127      bank_account 118766027194 662030224077 2025-01-29 DEO04     


There are 11 changes. A change of bank account is normal. Banks merge and firms move. Two patterns are not normal. The first is a change that is reversed soon after. We find it by joining the log to itself. A change is reversed if a later change of the same vendor puts back the old account.

reversed <- vendor_changes |>
  inner_join(vendor_changes |> select(vendor_id, back_on = changed_on, back_to = new_value, back_by = changed_by),
             by = join_by(vendor_id, old_value == back_to, changed_on < back_on)) |>
  mutate(days_held = as.numeric(back_on - changed_on))

reversed |>
  select(vendor_id, changed_on, back_on, days_held, changed_by, back_by)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  vendor_id changed_on back_on    days_held changed_by back_by
  <chr>     <date>     <date>         <dbl> <chr>      <chr>  
1 V127      2025-01-17 2025-01-29        12 DEO04      DEO04  


One vendor, V127, Narmada Office Solutions, had its account changed on 17 January 2025 and changed back 12 days later. Both changes were made by the same user, DEO04. The second pattern is a payment soon after a change, especially one much larger than the vendor’s usual payment. We join each payment to any change of the same vendor in the 15 days before it, and compare the amount with the vendor’s median payment.

usual <- payments |>
  summarise(usual_payment = median(amount), .by = vendor_id)

after_change <- payments |>
  inner_join(vendor_changes |> mutate(window_end = changed_on + 15) |>
               select(vendor_id, changed_on, window_end, new_value),
             by = join_by(vendor_id, between(pay_date, changed_on, window_end))) |>
  left_join(usual, by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(days_after = as.numeric(pay_date - changed_on),
         times_usual = round(amount / usual_payment, 1))

after_change |>
  select(vendor_id, changed_on, pay_date, days_after, amount, times_usual, paid_to_account)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  vendor_id changed_on pay_date   days_after  amount times_usual paid_to_account
  <chr>     <date>     <date>          <dbl>   <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>          
1 V179      2024-10-24 2024-10-31          7  7.95e4         1.3 662084840488   
2 V158      2024-12-18 2024-12-23          5  4.94e4         0.5 502183006249   
3 V127      2025-01-17 2025-01-20          3  1.36e6        30.5 118766027194   
4 V127      2025-01-29 2025-02-03          5  4.32e4         1   662030224077   


4 payments came within 15 days of a change. 3 of them are ordinary payments, no larger than about 1.3 times the vendor’s usual amount, into the account then in force. One stands out. On 20 January 2025, 3 days after the change, Narmada Office Solutions was paid ₹13.6 lakh, about 30 times its usual payment, into the account that lasted 12 days. We follow this case in Section 6.9.

f_bank <- unique(c(reversed$vendor_id, after_change$vendor_id[after_change$times_usual >= 3]))


6.4.4 Duplicate vendors
A PAN belongs to one person or firm, and so does a bank account. Two vendor records with the same PAN, or the same bank account, may be one vendor entered twice. A duplicate record lets the same bill be paid twice, once to each record, and the duplicate checks of Chapter 34, which work within a vendor, will not see it. filter(n() > 1, .by = ) keeps the groups with more than one row.

vendors |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = pan) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, pan, gstin, bank_account, created_on)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  vendor_id vendor_name                pan        gstin  bank_account created_on
  <chr>     <chr>                      <chr>      <chr>  <chr>        <date>    
1 V204      Kaveri Electricals         JYGCK3173N 22JYG… 118718879548 2015-01-12
2 V226      Maa Durga Medical Agencies BBVFM1825R 22BBV… 502128866750 2017-02-14
3 V259      Kaveri Electricals         JYGCK3173N 22JYG… 118718879548 2021-07-05
4 V293      Maa Durga Medical Agency   BBVFM1825R 22BBV… 502155620648 2024-06-20

vendors |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = bank_account) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, bank_account, address)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  vendor_id vendor_name        bank_account address                             
  <chr>     <chr>              <chr>        <chr>                               
1 V204      Kaveri Electricals 118718879548 Plot 3, Industrial Area, Rajdhani N…
2 V259      Kaveri Electricals 118718879548 Shop No. 18, Gandhi Market, Chandga…


Two pairs share a PAN. The two records of Kaveri Electricals also share a bank account, but they have different GSTINs. The thirteenth character of a GSTIN counts the registrations of one PAN in a State, so 1 and 2 mean two genuine registrations, here for two places of business. That is a known and harmless reason. The Maa Durga pair is different. The names differ by one letter, the bank accounts differ, and the second record was registered only in June 2024. A second record with a new bank account is exactly what a duplicate payment needs.

f_duppan <- vendors |> filter(n() > 1, .by = pan) |> pull(vendor_id)


6.4.5 Vendors linked to employees
An employee who owns or controls a vendor has a conflict of interest. The link often shows in the data as a shared bank account, PAN or address. Section 55.5 found such links, including indirect ones, with a network. Here a direct check is enough. We compare each of the three fields, after removing spaces and punctuation and changing to lower case, so that small differences in writing do not hide a match.

clean_value <- function(x) str_to_lower(str_remove_all(x, "[^A-Za-z0-9]"))

link_on <- function(field) {
  inner_join(vendors |> transmute(vendor_id, vendor_name, value = clean_value(.data[[field]])),
             employees |> transmute(emp_id, emp_name, office, designation, value = clean_value(.data[[field]])),
             by = "value") |>
    mutate(shared = field)
}

emp_links <- map(c("bank_account", "pan", "address"), link_on) |>
  list_rbind()

emp_links |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, emp_id, emp_name, office, designation, shared)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  vendor_id vendor_name          emp_id emp_name     office   designation shared
  <chr>     <chr>                <chr>  <chr>        <chr>    <chr>       <chr> 
1 V221      Sagar Lighting House E1012  Anita Pandey Madhopur Junior Eng… bank_…


.data[[field]] picks the column whose name is held in field, so one function serves all three fields. map() runs it for each field and list_rbind() stacks the results. One vendor, Sagar Lighting House, is paid into the bank account of Anita Pandey, a Junior Engineer of the Madhopur office. It received ₹14.7 lakh in the year. There may be an innocent reason, such as a relative’s firm that once used the account. But a vendor paid into an employee’s account must be explained, and the employee’s role in its orders must be checked.

f_emp <- unique(emp_links$vendor_id)







WarningCaution, privacy of employee and vendor data



This chapter joins the bank accounts, PANs and addresses of employees with those of vendors. These are personal data. Use them only for the audit, keep them in a protected folder, and do not put full account numbers or PANs in the report. Mask them, or use the vendor and employee ids. Chapter 9 explains how to mask, pseudonymise and store such data safely. A name in a list of flags is not a finding against that person, so share such lists only with those who need them.



6.4.6 PAN and GSTIN
A PAN has a fixed format, and a GSTIN has a check character. Section 21.10 and Section 21.11 explained both. We reuse the GSTIN check in a compact form. A valid GSTIN must also contain the vendor’s own PAN, in characters 3 to 12.

gst_chars <- c(0:9, LETTERS)
gstin_valid <- function(x) {
  map_lgl(x, function(g) {
    if (is.na(g) || !str_detect(g, "^[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$")) return(FALSE)
    v <- match(strsplit(str_sub(g, 1, 14), "")[[1]], gst_chars) - 1
    p <- v * rep(c(1, 2), 7)
    total <- sum(p %/% 36 + p %% 36)
    gst_chars[((36 - total %% 36) %% 36) + 1] == str_sub(g, 15, 15)
  })
}

id_check <- vendors |>
  mutate(pan_ok = str_detect(pan, "^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$"),
         gstin_ok = if_else(is.na(gstin), NA, gstin_valid(gstin)),
         gstin_has_pan = str_sub(gstin, 3, 12) == pan)

id_check |>
  filter(!pan_ok | !gstin_ok | !gstin_has_pan) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, pan, gstin, gstin_ok, gstin_has_pan)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  vendor_id vendor_name        pan        gstin           gstin_ok gstin_has_pan
  <chr>     <chr>              <chr>      <chr>           <lgl>    <lgl>        
1 V180      Pragati Paper Mart FDOFP3278K 22FDOFP3478K1ZJ FALSE    FALSE        


Every PAN has the right format. One GSTIN, of Pragati Paper Mart, fails the check, and the PAN inside it does not match the vendor’s PAN. They differ in one character. It is probably a typing error in the master. But a wrong GSTIN means that the department’s tax records point to the wrong taxpayer, and any tax credit claimed on these bills is at risk. It should be corrected from the vendor’s registration certificate, and verified on the GST portal.

f_ids <- bad_id$vendor_id


6.4.7 Large payments to vendors with no GSTIN
A supplier must register under GST once its turnover crosses a limit set by the law. Small local suppliers often have no GSTIN, and that is normal. But a vendor that sells a large amount to one department alone, with no GSTIN, deserves a question. Either it is registered and the master is incomplete, or it is not registered when it may need to be. We do not test the legal limit here, which depends on the kind of supply and the State. We simply list unregistered vendors paid more than a working threshold of ₹10 lakh, chosen by the audit team.

no_gstin <- vendors |>
  filter(is.na(gstin)) |>
  left_join(vendor_paid, by = "vendor_id") |>
  arrange(desc(paid))

no_gstin |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, created_on, payments, paid) |>
  head(5)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  vendor_id vendor_name               created_on payments     paid
  <chr>     <chr>                     <date>        <int>    <dbl>
1 V189      Trinetra Medical Agencies 2024-11-04        5 3698200 
2 V121      Saraswati Paper Mart      2023-03-05       10  395070.
3 V206      Satpura Electricals       2023-07-11        9  329190.
4 V276      Nilgiri Paper Mart        2019-01-14        6  199130.
5 V194      Anand Surgicals           2023-06-18        5  185872.


17 vendors have no GSTIN. All but one were paid less than ₹4 lakh each in the year, or nothing. The exception is Trinetra Medical Agencies, paid ₹37 lakh, the same vendor that was paid within a week of registration.

f_nogst <- no_gstin$vendor_id[coalesce(no_gstin$paid, 0) > 10e5]

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
text:
6.5 The three-way match
The oldest control in payables is the three-way match. Before a bill is paid, three documents must agree. The purchase order says what was ordered and at what rate. The goods receipt says what actually arrived. The invoice says what the vendor is charging. The office should pay for the quantity received, at the rate ordered, and nothing more. Any difference must be explained before payment.
Let us see it on a tiny example of three orders.

t_po  <- tribble(~po_no, ~po_date,     ~qty, ~rate,
                 "P1",   "2024-06-01", 100,  50,
                 "P2",   "2024-06-03", 200,  20,
                 "P3",   "2024-06-05", 50,   80)
t_grn <- tribble(~po_no, ~received_on, ~qty_received,
                 "P1",   "2024-06-10", 100,
                 "P2",   "2024-06-12", 150,
                 "P3",   "2024-06-25", 50)
t_inv <- tribble(~inv, ~po_no, ~inv_qty, ~inv_rate, ~paid_on,
                 "B1", "P1",   100,      50,        "2024-06-15",
                 "B2", "P2",   200,      20,        "2024-06-20",
                 "B3", "P3",   50,       90,        "2024-06-18")

t_inv |>
  left_join(t_po, by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(t_grn, by = "po_no") |>
  mutate(billed_over_received = inv_qty > qty_received,
         rate_above_order = inv_rate > rate,
         paid_before_receipt = paid_on < received_on)

# A tibble: 3 × 13
  inv   po_no inv_qty inv_rate paid_on    po_date      qty  rate received_on
  <chr> <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
1 B1    P1        100       50 2024-06-15 2024-06-01   100    50 2024-06-10 
2 B2    P2        200       20 2024-06-20 2024-06-03   200    20 2024-06-12 
3 B3    P3         50       90 2024-06-18 2024-06-05    50    80 2024-06-25 
# ℹ 4 more variables: qty_received <dbl>, billed_over_received <lgl>,
#   rate_above_order <lgl>, paid_before_receipt <lgl>


The dates are text here, but in the form year-month-day, text compares in the right order. Bill B1 matches. Bill B2 charges for 200 units when 150 arrived. Bill B3 charges ₹90 against an order at ₹80, and was paid a week before the goods came. Each test is one comparison after two joins. Now the real data. Some orders arrive in two deliveries, so we first total the receipts of each order. We keep the first and last challan dates and the last date of entry.

received <- receipts |>
  summarise(qty_received = sum(qty_received), last_challan = max(challan_date),
            last_grn = max(grn_date), .by = po_no)

paid_inv <- payments |>
  summarise(paid = sum(amount), pay_date = min(pay_date), .by = inv_id)

match3 <- invoices |>
  left_join(select(purchase_orders, po_no, po_date, po_qty = qty, po_rate = rate), by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(received, by = "po_no") |>
  left_join(paid_inv, by = "inv_id")

match3 |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, po_no, po_qty, qty_received, inv_qty, po_rate, inv_rate, pay_date)

# A tibble: 1,089 × 9
   inv_id   vendor_id po_no         po_qty qty_received inv_qty po_rate inv_rate
   <chr>    <chr>     <chr>          <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
 1 INV00001 V132      PO/24-25/0035    347          347     347   380      380  
 2 INV00002 V137      PO/24-25/0005     11           11      11  3714.    3714. 
 3 INV00003 V175      PO/24-25/0009   4896         4896    4896    19.9     19.9
 4 INV00004 V261      PO/24-25/0012    152          152     152   246.     246. 
 5 INV00005 V136      PO/24-25/0013   2176         2176    2176    18.3     18.3

10 INV00010 V179      PO/24-25/0031     33           33      33   430.     430. 
# ℹ 1,079 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: pay_date <date>


match3 has one row for each invoice, with its order, receipts and payment beside it. 16 invoices are not yet paid, and show NA in the payment columns. They are the payables at the year end. Now the six tests.

6.5.1 Invoices with no order

no_order <- match3 |>
  filter(is.na(po_no))

no_order |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, office, item, inv_date, inv_qty, amount, pay_date)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  inv_id   vendor_id office    item         inv_date   inv_qty amount pay_date  
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>     <chr>        <date>       <dbl>  <dbl> <date>    
1 INV00056 V293      Sitapur   Surgical gl… 2024-05-01      71 3.02e4 2024-06-25
2 INV00404 V192      Chandgarh Cement bag   2024-08-19     300 1.14e5 2024-09-12
3 INV00562 V204      Chandgarh LED bulb 9W  2024-10-03     150 1.56e4 2024-10-19
4 INV00676 V192      Chandgarh Cement bag   2024-11-07     280 1.06e5 2024-11-29
5 INV00916 V192      Chandgarh Cement bag   2025-01-16     320 1.14e5 2025-02-11
6 INV01043 V192      Chandgarh Cement bag   2025-02-27     260 9.23e4 2025-03-14


6 invoices were paid with no order. 4 are bills of Jai Ambe Cement Depot for cement at Chandgarh, spread through the year. A bill with no order may be a genuine emergency purchase, approved later. Four from one vendor at one office look like a habit. There is also a bill of Maa Durga Medical Agency, the duplicate vendor, which we meet again in Section 6.7.

6.5.2 Invoices dated before the order
An invoice cannot normally come before the order. When it does, the order was probably raised after the purchase, to regularise it. This is called a post facto order.

before_order <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_date < po_date) |>
  mutate(days_before = as.numeric(po_date - inv_date))

before_order |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, po_no, po_date, inv_date, days_before, amount)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  inv_id   vendor_id po_no         po_date    inv_date   days_before  amount

4 INV00502 V186      PO/24-25/0584 2024-09-26 2024-09-17           9  88231.


4 invoices, from 4 vendors, are dated 5 to 11 days before their orders. They may be honest regularisations of urgent purchases. They are still a breach of procedure, and worth a line in the report if they are frequent.

6.5.3 More billed than received

over_billed <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_qty > qty_received) |>
  mutate(short = inv_qty - qty_received, value_short = short * inv_rate)

over_billed |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_qty, qty_received, inv_qty, short, value_short)

  inv_id   vendor_id item          po_qty qty_received inv_qty short value_short

1 INV00104 V192      Cement bag       223          183     223    40       15200
2 INV00236 V192      Cement bag       159          124     159    35       13300

4 INV00849 V189      Surgical glo…   2000         1200    2000   800      364000
5 INV01008 V189      Surgical glo…   2000         1100    2000   900      414000
6 INV01058 V192      Cement bag       263          233     263    30       10650


6 invoices charge for more than arrived. 4 are cement bills of Jai Ambe Cement Depot, each short by 30 to 50 bags. Short deliveries of cement are hard to see at the site and easy to hide. 2 are bills of Trinetra Medical Agencies for surgical gloves, where the whole order was billed but only part arrived.

6.5.4 Rate billed above the order

rate_above <- match3 |>
  filter(inv_rate > po_rate + 0.005) |>
  mutate(pct_above = round(100 * (inv_rate / po_rate - 1), 1),
         extra = (inv_rate - po_rate) * inv_qty)

rate_above |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_rate, inv_rate, pct_above, extra)

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  inv_id   vendor_id item         po_rate inv_rate pct_above  extra
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>
1 INV00215 V133      Office chair   5450     6104         12  7848 
2 INV00291 V133      Office chair   5555.    6388         15 11665.
3 INV00324 V133      Office chair   5624.    6186.        10  3374.


We allow half a paisa for rounding. 3 bills of Shiv Shakti Steel Furniture charge 10% to 15% above the order rate for chairs. The extra is small, ₹22,887 in all. But the control should have stopped it, and it did not.

6.5.5 Paid before the goods arrived
Payment should follow receipt. Here two dates matter. The challan date is when the goods arrived. The GRN date is when the store entered them in the system. Let us flag payments made before the last GRN date, and show both dates.

paid_early <- match3 |>
  filter(pay_date < last_grn) |>
  mutate(goods_arrived_after_payment = last_challan > pay_date)

paid_early |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, pay_date, last_challan, last_grn, goods_arrived_after_payment, amount)

# A tibble: 8 × 8
  inv_id   vendor_id item            pay_date   last_challan last_grn  
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>           <date>     <date>       <date>    
1 INV00131 V258      LED bulb 9W     2024-06-15 2024-05-26   2024-06-24
2 INV00196 V117      LED bulb 9W     2024-07-11 2024-06-15   2024-07-18
3 INV00445 V237      Cement bag      2024-09-11 2024-08-31   2024-09-21
4 INV00593 V137      Toner cartridge 2024-10-15 2024-10-24   2024-10-24
5 INV00780 V223      LED bulb 9W     2024-12-20 2024-12-07   2024-12-25
6 INV00787 V158      Cement bag      2024-12-23 2024-12-08   2025-01-02
7 INV01045 V170      Office chair    2025-03-02 2025-03-14   2025-03-14
8 INV01073 V170      Office chair    2025-03-09 2025-03-24   2025-03-24
# ℹ 2 more variables: goods_arrived_after_payment <lgl>, amount <dbl>


8 invoices were paid before the receipt was entered. But in 5 of them, the challan shows that the goods had arrived before payment. The store simply entered the receipt late. That is a weakness in record keeping, not an advance payment. In the other 3, the goods arrived after payment, worth ₹16.5 lakh. 2 of these are the chairs of Gomti Furniture House, the dormant vendor, paid two days after billing and received weeks later.






WarningCaution, a mismatch may be a recording delay



Many breaks in the three-way match are only breaks in the records. A receipt entered late, an invoice keyed in with the wrong date, or an order amended after delivery all look like exceptions. Before treating one as a finding, look at the paper. Here the challan date separated a late entry from a real advance payment. In other data, the store register, the gate entry book or the vendor’s delivery note may do the same. If late entries are common, that is itself a point to report, because the system cannot then be relied on to block payment before receipt.



6.5.6 Paid in full for part of the order
The tests above look at one document against another. A final check looks at the money. For each invoice, what was paid, and what were the goods actually received worth at the order rate? The difference is the amount paid for nothing.

paid_over <- match3 |>
  filter(!is.na(paid)) |>
  mutate(value_received = qty_received * po_rate,
         paid_for_nothing = round(paid - value_received, 2)) |>
  filter(paid_for_nothing > 1)

paid_over |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, item, po_qty, qty_received, paid, value_received, paid_for_nothing)

# A tibble: 9 × 8
  inv_id   vendor_id item            po_qty qty_received    paid value_received
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>            <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>          <dbl>
1 INV00104 V192      Cement bag         223          183  84740          69540 
2 INV00215 V133      Office chair        12           12  73248          65400 
3 INV00236 V192      Cement bag         159          124  60420          47120 
4 INV00291 V133      Office chair        14           14  89432          77767.
5 INV00324 V133      Office chair         6            6  37118.         33744.
6 INV00732 V192      Cement bag         124           74  47120          28120 
7 INV00849 V189      Surgical gloves   2000         1200 910000         546000 
8 INV01008 V189      Surgical gloves   2000         1100 920000         506000 
9 INV01058 V192      Cement bag         263          233  93365          82715 
# ℹ 1 more variable: paid_for_nothing <dbl>


9 paid invoices exceed the value received, by ₹8.6 lakh in all. This one test catches both short delivery and rates above the order. The two gloves orders of Trinetra Medical Agencies account for ₹7.8 lakh. Each order was received in part but paid in full. Invoices with no order do not appear here, since they have no order rate. They need the test of Section 6.5.1.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
text:
6.6 Price benchmarking
The three-way match checks that the office paid the price it agreed. It cannot tell whether that price was reasonable. For that we compare each purchase with other purchases of the same item. When eight offices buy the same toner cartridge, most of them pay roughly the same. One office paying much more is worth a question.
The fair comparison is with the median price of the same item in the same period. The median is not pulled by the few extreme prices we are looking for, as Section 50.4 explained. Let us see the idea on six purchases of one item in one quarter.

tiny <- tibble(office = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"),
               rate = c(3400, 3450, 3380, 3520, 4760, 3410))
tiny |>
  mutate(median_rate = median(rate), ratio = round(rate / median_rate, 2))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  office  rate median_rate ratio
  <chr>  <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 A       3400        3430  0.99
2 B       3450        3430  1.01
3 C       3380        3430  0.99
4 D       3520        3430  1.03
5 E       4760        3430  1.39
6 F       3410        3430  0.99


The median is ₹3430. Office E pays 1.39 times the median, about 39% more. The others are within a few per cent. Now for every order. We compare like with like, the same item in the same quarter of the financial year. quarter() with fiscal_start = 4 numbers the quarters from April.

bench <- purchase_orders |>
  mutate(qtr = quarter(po_date, fiscal_start = 4)) |>
  mutate(median_rate = median(rate), orders = n(), .by = c(item, qtr)) |>
  mutate(ratio = rate / median_rate)

bench |>
  summarise(orders = n(), lowest = round(min(ratio), 2), highest = round(max(ratio), 2),
            above_25pct = sum(ratio > 1.25), .by = item)

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  item               orders lowest highest above_25pct
  <chr>               <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>       <int>
1 Toner cartridge       156   0.88    1.42          19
2 A4 paper              237   0.87    1.16           0
3 LED bulb 9W           179   0.88    1.12           0
4 Paracetamol 500 mg    167   0.86    1.13           0
5 Office chair           68   0.89    1.16           0
6 Surgical gloves       166   0.84    1.15           0
7 Cement bag            110   1       1.07           0


For every item except toner, the highest order is at most 16% above the median of its quarter. That is the normal spread from transport, quantity and timing. Cement shows no spread at all, since it is bought at the rate contract. Figure 6.1 shows each order against its median.

bench |>
  ggplot(aes(ratio, item)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, width = 0, alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.25, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Rate as a ratio of the median for the item and quarter", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()






Figure 6.1: Rate of each purchase order as a ratio of the median rate for the same item and quarter. The dashed line is 25% above the median. Only toner cartridges have orders above it.




Let us list the orders more than 25% above the median, by office, item and vendor.

high_price <- bench |>
  filter(ratio > 1.25)

high_price |>
  summarise(orders = n(), median_ratio = round(median(ratio), 2),
            .by = c(office, item, vendor_id))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  office  item            vendor_id orders median_ratio
  <chr>   <chr>           <chr>      <int>        <dbl>
1 Dhanpur Toner cartridge V169          19         1.37


All 19 orders are from one office, Dhanpur, for toner cartridges, from one vendor, Unnati Computer Supplies. The typical order is 37% above the median.

6.6.1 The excess paid
How much more did the office pay than the median price? For each flagged order, the excess is the difference between its rate and the median, times the quantity.

excess <- high_price |>
  mutate(excess = (rate - median_rate) * qty) |>
  summarise(orders = n(), quantity = sum(qty), paid = sum(rate * qty), excess = sum(excess),
            .by = c(office, item, vendor_id))
excess

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  office  item            vendor_id orders quantity     paid  excess
  <chr>   <chr>           <chr>      <int>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Dhanpur Toner cartridge V169          19      247 1247374. 342211.


At the median rate, these orders would have cost ₹3.4 lakh less. This is an estimate, not a loss. We should say so in those words.






WarningCaution, comparing like with like



A higher price is not always a worse price. Quality differs, as with an original toner cartridge against a compatible one. Small orders cost more per unit. Remote offices pay more for transport. Prices rise during the year, and in a shortage. So compare only the same item, of the same specification, in the same period. Use the median, not the lowest price, as the benchmark. Choose a margin that absorbs the normal spread, here 25%, and write it down before looking at the results. Then ask the office for its reasons before calling any difference excess. The excess is an estimate of what the department could have saved, and it is only as good as the comparison behind it.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
6  Payables and Vendors
section: 6.8 A risk view of each vendor
text:
6.8 A risk view of each vendor
We now have many flags, each pointing at some vendors. A vendor caught by one test may have a good reason. A vendor caught by several is a better use of the auditor’s time. As in Section 3.8, the simplest way to combine them is to count. Each test of the vendor master has already given a set of vendor ids. Let us collect the ids from the other tests in the same way.

f_three <- unique(c(no_order$vendor_id, before_order$vendor_id, over_billed$vendor_id,
                    rate_above$vendor_id, pe_real$vendor_id, paid_over$vendor_id))
f_price <- unique(high_price$vendor_id)
f_split <- unique(split_check$vendor_id)
f_oldrate <- unique(old_rate$vendor_id)

We put all the sets in one named list, and turn it into one row per vendor and test.

flag_lists <- list(
  new_and_paid_fast   = f_new,
  dormant_woke_up     = f_dormant,
  bank_change         = f_bank,
  same_pan            = f_duppan,
  employee_link       = f_emp,
  bad_gstin           = f_ids,
  no_gstin_large      = f_nogst,
  three_way_break     = f_three,
  price_above_median  = f_price,
  duplicate_bill      = f_dup,
  split_bills         = f_split,
  old_contract_rate   = f_oldrate
)

vendor_flags <- tibble(test = names(flag_lists), vendor_id = flag_lists) |>
  unnest(vendor_id) |>
  distinct()

risk <- vendor_flags |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = vendor_id) |>
  left_join(select(vendor_paid, vendor_id, paid), by = "vendor_id") |>
  mutate(vendor_name = vname(vendor_id), paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(vendor_id, vendor_name, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

risk |>
  print(n = 12)

# A tibble: 19 × 5
   vendor_id vendor_name                 flags paid_lakh tests                  
   <chr>     <chr>                       <int>     <dbl> <chr>                  
 1 V293      Maa Durga Medical Agency        4       1.5 new_and_paid_fast, sam…
 2 V189      Trinetra Medical Agencies       3      37   new_and_paid_fast, no_…
 3 V192      Jai Ambe Cement Depot           3      20.6 three_way_break, dupli…
 4 V170      Gomti Furniture House           2      16.1 dormant_woke_up, three…
 5 V221      Sagar Lighting House            2      14.7 employee_link, split_b…
 6 V226      Maa Durga Medical Agencies      2      10.3 same_pan, duplicate_bi…
 7 V204      Kaveri Electricals              2       4.9 same_pan, three_way_br…
 8 V127      Narmada Office Solutions        1      25.1 bank_change            
 9 V234      Vindhya Health Distributors     1      20.7 new_and_paid_fast      
10 V169      Unnati Computer Supplies        1      18.1 price_above_median     
11 V137      Mangal Paper Mart               1      14   three_way_break        
12 V132      Navin Hardware Stores           1      13   three_way_break        
# ℹ 7 more rows


tibble() with a list column, followed by unnest(), turns the named list into a long table. 19 of 193 vendors raise at least one flag, and 7 raise two or more. Those with two or more are nearly all planted cases. Two are not. The genuine Maa Durga Medical Agencies is flagged only because of its twin. One of the Kaveri records shares a PAN for a known reason, and has one bill without an order. Some serious cases raise only one flag. Narmada’s bank change and Dhanpur’s toner vendor are examples. So the count is a way to order the work, not a filter that decides what to ignore.
A count treats every test as equal. They are not. A bank account shared with an employee is more serious than an invoice dated a few days before its order. Section 1.8 gave each test a weight. Weights are a judgement. If they are used, the audit team should fix them before looking at the results, and write down the reason for each. It should also check that the ranking does not change much with other sensible weights. The count also ignores money. A vendor with two flags and ₹50 lakh of payments may matter more than one with three flags and ₹50,000.






NoteA flag is a lead



None of these tests proves a fraud. Each one says where to look. The work that follows is ordinary audit work. Read the file, see the goods, talk to the people, and confirm with the vendor or the bank. The value of the analysis is that it tests every vendor and every bill, and so points that work at the right places.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
section: 6.9 Audit use case, a vendor whose bank account changed before a large payment
text:
6.9 Audit use case, a vendor whose bank account changed before a large payment
Let us follow Narmada Office Solutions. First, its whole history in the change log and its payments, side by side.

vendor_changes |>
  filter(vendor_id == nar_id) |>
  select(changed_on, old_value, new_value, changed_by)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  changed_on old_value    new_value    changed_by
  <date>     <chr>        <chr>        <chr>     
1 2025-01-17 662030224077 118766027194 DEO04     
2 2025-01-29 118766027194 662030224077 DEO04     

payments |>
  filter(vendor_id == nar_id, pay_date >= as.Date("2024-12-01")) |>
  left_join(select(invoices, inv_id, inv_no, item, inv_qty, po_no), by = "inv_id") |>
  select(pay_id, pay_date, inv_no, item, inv_qty, amount, paid_to_account)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  pay_id   pay_date   inv_no  item     inv_qty   amount paid_to_account
  <chr>    <date>     <chr>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>          
1 PAY00690 2024-12-02 NOS/952 A4 paper     154   41016. 662030224077   
2 PAY00862 2025-01-20 NOS/458 A4 paper    5200 1362400  118766027194   
3 PAY00912 2025-02-03 NOS/647 A4 paper     148   43231. 662030224077   
4 PAY00953 2025-02-17 NOS/291 A4 paper     159   44730. 662030224077   
5 PAY01056 2025-03-23 NOS/708 A4 paper     192   54741. 662030224077   


The story is clear. The vendor usually receives about ₹44,730 a payment. On 17 January 2025 user DEO04 changed its account. Three days later, on 20 January 2025, it was paid ₹13.6 lakh for an order of 5,200 reams of paper, into the new account. On 29 January 2025 the same user put the old account back. Every other payment, before and after, went to the old account.
Does the temporary account appear anywhere else? We check it against the vendor master, the employee master and all payments.

c(in_vendor_master   = sum(vendors$bank_account == temp_acct),
  in_employee_master = sum(employees$bank_account == temp_acct),
  payments_into_it   = sum(payments$paid_to_account == temp_acct))

  in_vendor_master in_employee_master   payments_into_it 
                 0                  0                  1 


The account belongs to no other vendor or employee in our data, and received only this one payment. User DEO04 made 2 changes in the whole year, these two and no others.
The order itself passed the three-way match. The paper was ordered, received and billed at the order rate. So the question is not whether the department owed the money. It is whether the money reached the vendor.

6.9.1 What the auditor does next

Ask the department for the request behind each change. A genuine change comes with a letter from the vendor and a cancelled cheque or bank certificate. Check who verified it, and how.

Confirm with the vendor, directly and not through the office, whether it received ₹13.6 lakh in January 2025, and into which account.
Ask the bank, through the department, for the name of the holder of the temporary account.
Find out why DEO04 had the right to change bank details, and whether any second person approved the change. A system that lets one user change an account without approval is a control weakness in itself, whatever the outcome of this case.
Widen the test. Ask for the change log of earlier years, and for changes of other fields, such as the address or mobile number to which payment advices are sent.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
section: 6.10 Audit use case, one office paying more for the same item
text:
6.10 Audit use case, one office paying more for the same item
Let us look closer at toner cartridges. Is Dhanpur’s high price steady through the year, or a passing spike? Figure 6.2 shows the rate of each toner order by date, with Dhanpur’s orders marked.

purchase_orders |>
  filter(item == "Toner cartridge") |>
  mutate(buyer = if_else(office == "Dhanpur", "Dhanpur", "Other offices")) |>
  ggplot(aes(po_date, rate, colour = buyer)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Dhanpur = "firebrick", "Other offices" = "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Order date", y = "Rate per cartridge (₹)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()






Figure 6.2: Rate of each order of toner cartridges in 2024-25. Dhanpur’s orders, all from one vendor, are well above those of the other offices throughout the year.




The gap is steady across the year. Let us compare Dhanpur with the other offices, quarter by quarter, and see which vendors each uses.

bench |>
  filter(item == "Toner cartridge") |>
  mutate(buyer = if_else(office == "Dhanpur", "Dhanpur", "Other offices")) |>
  summarise(orders = n(), median_rate = round(median(rate)), vendors = n_distinct(vendor_id),
            .by = c(qtr, buyer)) |>
  arrange(qtr, buyer)

# A tibble: 8 × 5
    qtr buyer         orders median_rate vendors
  <int> <chr>          <int>       <dbl>   <int>
1     1 Dhanpur            4        4865       1
2     1 Other offices     40        3559      14
3     2 Dhanpur            2        4990       1
4     2 Other offices     33        3596      14
5     3 Dhanpur           11        5028       1
6     3 Other offices     40        3610      15
7     4 Dhanpur            2        5141       1
8     4 Other offices     24        3729      12


In every quarter, Dhanpur pays about 39% more than the median of the other offices, and buys from only one vendor. Could the order sizes explain it? The median Dhanpur order is for 11 cartridges, against 11 elsewhere, so quantity does not explain it. Could distance explain it? For all its other items, Dhanpur’s orders sit at the median, with a typical ratio of 1.00, so its transport costs are ordinary. Most telling of all, Unnati Computer Supplies also sells toner to 1 other office, at a median of ₹3,462 a cartridge. The same vendor charges Dhanpur far more than it charges others.
The estimate of excess is ₹3.4 lakh over the year. The total is modest. The pattern is what matters. One office, one vendor, one item, the whole year.

6.10.1 What the auditor does next

Ask the Dhanpur office how the vendor was chosen and how the rate was fixed. Was there a quotation, a tender or a rate contract? Were other vendors invited? Link to Chapter 3 if there was a tender.
Compare the specification. If Dhanpur buys original cartridges and others buy compatible ones, the difference may be fair, though the choice itself may then need a reason. Check the printers in use.

Inspect the stock and the issue register, to see that the cartridges bought were received and used.
Check the vendor’s other links. Is it linked to any employee of the office, through the tests of Section 6.4.5 or a network as in Section 55.5?
Report the excess as an estimate, with the method, the benchmark, the margin and the cautions, and invite the department’s reply.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
text:
6.11 A suggested workflow


Get the full purchase-to-pay data, including the vendor change log, employee master and earlier years’ payments. Record who extracted it and when.

Check completeness. Unique keys, every payment linked to an invoice and a vendor, and monthly totals agreeing with the bank.

Review the vendor master. New vendors paid fast, dormant vendors woken up, bank changes near payments and reversed changes, duplicate PANs and bank accounts, links with employees, PAN and GSTIN checks, and large payments to vendors with no GSTIN.

Run the three-way match on every invoice. No order, invoice before order, more billed than received, rate above the order, payment before receipt, and paid more than the value received.

Separate recording delays from real breaks, using challan dates or other evidence, before treating any break as an exception.

Benchmark prices against the median of the same item and period, with a margin fixed in advance. Estimate the excess, and state it as an estimate.

Add the tests of earlier chapters. Duplicates, split bills, look-alike names, shared addresses and the rate in force.

Combine the flags by vendor, and rank. Use weights only with written reasons.

Follow up the top vendors with documents, inspection and confirmation, and record what cleared each flag.







ImportantRemember




The vendor master decides who can be paid. Review it, and its change log, before the transactions.
A bank account changed and changed back around one payment is one of the clearest signs of payment diversion. Only the change log shows it.
The three-way match asks three questions. Was it ordered, did it arrive, and does the bill agree? Payment should follow all three.
Many breaks are recording delays. Use a second date or a document to tell them apart.
Benchmark prices against the median of like purchases, and report the excess as an estimate, with its cautions.
One flag is often innocent. Several flags on one vendor deserve the auditor’s time.

title: 6  Payables and Vendors
text:
6.12 Where next
The duplicate tests are explained in Chapter 34, and the split bills in Section 15.17 and Chapter 33. String distances are in Chapter 35, and record linkage across whole files in Chapter 36. Employee and vendor links are shown as a network in Section 55.5, and vendors at the same place on a map in Section 57.7. PAN and GSTIN checks are in Section 21.10 and Section 21.11. Robust comparison with a median is explained in Section 50.4, and rolling joins for the rate in force in Section 16.6. The ledger behind these payments is tested in Chapter 1, the bank in Chapter 2, and the tenders in Chapter 3. Personal data in the masters must be handled as in Chapter 9.

These exercises use the tables and objects of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.


A wider window for new vendors. Using new_vendors, list the vendors paid within 60 days of registration. How many are there?

ex_new60

5 vendors were paid within 60 days, against 3 within a week. The extra ones were paid after 37 to 47 days, the normal time for an order, a delivery and a bill. A wider window catches more vendors, but mostly ordinary ones. The window is a choice, and should be written down.





Vendors sharing a bank account. Find the bank accounts used by more than one vendor, and the number of vendors on each.

ex_shared <- vendors |>
  count(bank_account, name = "vendors") |>

ex_shared

  bank_account vendors
  <chr>          <int>
1 118718879548       2


1 account is shared, by 2 vendors. They are the two registrations of Kaveri Electricals, which also share a PAN. Other shared accounts, with different PANs, would be far more serious.





Payables at the year end. Using match3, list the invoices not paid by 31 March 2025, with their total in ₹ lakh. Which is the oldest?






TipSolution






ex_unpaid <- match3 |>
  filter(is.na(paid)) |>
  arrange(inv_date)
nrow(ex_unpaid)

[1] 16

round(sum(ex_unpaid$amount) / 1e5, 1)

[1] 14.7

ex_unpaid |>
  select(inv_id, vendor_id, office, item, inv_date, amount) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  inv_id   vendor_id office      item            inv_date   amount
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>       <chr>           <date>      <dbl>
1 INV01040 V198      Dhanpur     Surgical gloves 2025-02-26 17287.
2 INV01041 V187      Keshavnagar Surgical gloves 2025-02-27 19748.
3 INV01051 V204      Chandgarh   LED bulb 9W     2025-03-01 57922.


16 invoices worth ₹14.7 lakh were unpaid at the year end. The oldest is dated 26 February 2025, only 33 days before the year end. Unpaid bills are liabilities that should appear in the department’s accounts. Old ones may point to disputes, or to bills held back for a reason worth knowing.





A tighter price margin. Repeat the benchmark with a margin of 15% instead of 25%. How many orders are flagged now, and from which offices and items?






TipSolution






ex_15 <- bench |>
  filter(ratio > 1.15) |>
  count(office, item, name = "orders")
ex_15

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  office   item            orders
  <chr>    <chr>            <int>
1 Dhanpur  A4 paper             1
2 Dhanpur  Toner cartridge     19
3 Ratanpur Office chair         1


21 orders are flagged, against 19 at 25%. The extra 2 are single orders, of A4 paper at Dhanpur and of office chair at Ratanpur. They are the normal spread of transport and order size, which the wider margin was chosen to absorb.





Robust z-scores for toner. Using bench, compute the robust z-score of each toner order within its quarter, as in Section 50.4, with median() and mad(). How many orders have a robust z-score above 3.5, and from which office?






TipSolution






ex_rz <- bench |>
  filter(item == "Toner cartridge") |>
  mutate(rz = (rate - median(rate)) / mad(rate), .by = qtr) |>
  filter(rz > 3.5)
ex_rz |>
  count(office, vendor_id)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  office   vendor_id     n
  <chr>    <chr>     <int>
1 Dhanpur  V169         19
2 Ratanpur V214          1


20 orders have a robust z-score above 3.5. 19 are Dhanpur’s. The other is an order of Ratanpur, only 13% above the median. Toner prices of other offices vary little, so the MAD is small, and even a modest difference gives a large score. The robust z-score measures distance in units of the usual spread. The ratio to the median is easier to explain in a report. For cement, where every order is at the contract rate, the MAD is zero and the score cannot be computed.

title: Part III. Pay and Revenue
text:
Pay and pensions are usually a department’s largest expenditure, and pensions are paid for decades. The payroll chapter tests both against the records that should support them. The revenue chapter then turns from money spent to money that should have been collected.


7  Payroll and Pensions
A department’s payroll and pensions tested against the change log, sanctioned posts, attendance and life certificates, with a risk view of each person.


8  Revenue and Tax
A State tax on goods and services tested against movement records and buyers’ reports, with rates, thresholds, refunds, shell dealers, stamp duty and old demands.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
text:
7.1 Where payroll and pensions go wrong
A State Water Resources Department pays about nine hundred employees every month. Salaries are usually the largest expenditure of such a department, larger than all its purchases. After retirement the State pays them a pension, often for twenty or thirty years, and then a family pension to the spouse. So one wrong entry in a master is repeated every month, sometimes for decades. A clerk who never existed draws a salary in one office. A pensioner who died years ago is still paid, because nobody asked for the life certificate. Each shows only when the payroll is read against another record.
Earlier chapters already hold many payroll and pension tests, such as the pay bill rule book of Chapter 31 and the pensioners found dead in Chapter 36. This chapter runs them together for one department, in a few lines each. It then adds what the book lacks. These are a review of changes in the employee master, a check of the payroll against sanctioned strength and attendance, and a set of pension tests. Finally it combines the flags for each employee and pensioner, and follows two cases to the end.
As in every chapter of this part, a flag is not a finding. Many flags in payroll have an innocent cause, such as leave, deputation or an order entered late. The aim is to find the few that need a question.
Prerequisites
Pay and pension pass through a few records, and each can be checked against the others.
The controls are simple. Nobody should be paid unless the person exists, holds a sanctioned post, is in service that month and is paid at a rate an order allows. A pensioner should be paid only while alive, and only what the rules give.
