title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
section: 7.2 Our data, the payroll and pensions of a State water resources department
text:
7.2 Our data, the payroll and pensions of a State water resources department
Our auditee is an imaginary Water Resources Department of a State, with a head office and eight division offices. We have its payroll and pension records for 2024-25. All names and numbers are made up. There are thirteen tables.


employees is the employee master, with dates of birth, joining and leaving, PAN, bank account and mobile number.

master_changes is its change log. It records each change of basic pay or bank account, with the order number and the user.

payroll has one row per employee per month. It holds the days paid, basic pay, dearness allowance (DA), house rent allowance (HRA), other allowances, deductions, net pay and the account credited.

arrears holds the supplementary bills for arrears, with the period covered.

sanctioned holds the posts of each cadre in each office, and attendance a monthly summary of days present and on leave.

pensioners is the pension master, with the pension payment order (PPO) number, type of pension, last pay, monthly pension and any date of death. A family pension carries the PPO of the pension it follows, in linked_ppo.

pension_paid holds the monthly payments, life_certs the life certificates and commutation the lump sums paid on commuting part of a pension.

bank_salary and treasury_pension hold monthly totals from the bank and the treasury.

oap is the welfare department’s old age pension list.

Pay follows a few example norms. DA is 50% of basic pay up to September 2024 and 53% from October 2024. HRA is 30%, 20% or 10% of basic pay in cities of class X, Y and Z. A service pension is half of the last pay drawn, and a family pension 30% of it, with a minimum of ₹9,000. Employees retire at the end of the month in which they reach 60. These are illustrative rules for this example only. In real work, apply the actual rules and rates of your government.
Most of the data is routine. Employees join mid-month and leave. Some increments were entered late and paid as arrears. A few employees were on long leave, and two engineers are on deputation to the head office. Some pensioners died and their spouses draw a family pension. A few pensioners are over a hundred, and some sent their life certificates late. Into this, these cases have been planted.


Paid after leaving. A clerk of the Motinagar office who resigned on 31 August 2024 is paid for two more months.

Paid before joining. A Junior Engineer who joined at Amarpur in January 2025 is paid for December 2024 too.

A pay rise with no order. A clerk of Dhaulagarh has basic pay raised by more than a fifth, and the change log shows no order.

Two increments in a year. A senior clerk of Belkheda receives a second annual increment in January.

Arrears paid twice. The same arrears bill of one employee is paid again two months later.

A bank change just before arrears. An accountant’s account is changed four days before an arrears payment, and changed back ten days after it.

Ghost employees. Three clerks of Lakhanpur are paid every month but never attend. They share one mobile number.

A very old pensioner without a life certificate. A pensioner over 100 years old is paid all year, though his last life certificate is from 2021.

Family pension and service pension together. A pensioner died in July 2024. His widow is paid a family pension, and his own pension continues too.

Commutation paid twice, and a pension well above the rule.


The tests of earlier chapters will find a few more. Let us build the data.

Code to create the payroll and pension dataset.seed(2425)

fy_start <- as.Date("2024-04-01")
fy_end   <- as.Date("2025-03-31")
fy_months <- seq(fy_start, by = "month", length.out = 12)
month_end <- function(m) ceiling_date(m, "month") - 1

offices <- tibble(
  office     = c("Head Office", "Amarpur", "Belkheda", "Chandanpur", "Dhaulagarh",
                 "Kesargaon", "Lakhanpur", "Motinagar", "Sonpur"),
  city_class = c("X", "Y", "Z", "Y", "Z", "Z", "Y", "Z", "Y"))

cadres <- tribble(
  ~cadre,                ~level, ~min_pay, ~max_pay, ~div, ~ho,
  "Executive Engineer",  11,     67700,    208700,   1,    3,
  "Assistant Engineer",  10,     56100,    177500,   4,    6,
  "Junior Engineer",      6,     35400,    112400,   20,   0,
  "Accountant",           6,     35400,    112400,   3,    8,
  "Senior Clerk",         4,     25500,     81100,   8,    20,
  "Clerk",                2,     19900,     63200,   22,   36,
  "Driver",               2,     19900,     63200,   5,    8,
  "Multi-tasking staff",  1,     18000,     56900,   30,   24,
  "Gauge Reader",         1,     18000,     56900,   16,   0)

# ---- Names ----
male   <- c("Ramesh", "Suresh", "Mahesh", "Dinesh", "Rajendra", "Surendra", "Mukesh", "Rakesh",
            "Anil", "Sunil", "Vijay", "Ajay", "Sanjay", "Manoj", "Pramod", "Vinod", "Ashok",
            "Arvind", "Deepak", "Pankaj", "Rahul", "Amit", "Sumit", "Rohit", "Naveen", "Praveen",
            "Gopal", "Govind", "Kishore", "Hemant", "Yogesh", "Satish", "Harish", "Girish",
            "Shyam", "Mohan", "Ram Prakash", "Ram Kishore", "Jagdish", "Om Prakash", "Bhagwan Das",
            "Kailash", "Laxman", "Bharat", "Shankar", "Prem", "Devendra", "Narendra", "Lalit")
female <- c("Sunita", "Anita", "Kavita", "Savita", "Geeta", "Seema", "Rekha", "Asha", "Usha",
            "Meena", "Neha", "Pooja", "Priya", "Sarita", "Kiran", "Manju", "Anju", "Rita",
            "Shanti", "Kamla", "Vimla", "Sushila", "Pushpa", "Lalita", "Radha", "Sharda",
            "Kusum", "Saroj", "Nirmala", "Shobha", "Archana", "Vandana", "Rashmi", "Jyoti")
surname <- c("Sharma", "Verma", "Gupta", "Yadav", "Singh", "Patel", "Tiwari", "Mishra", "Pandey",
             "Chauhan", "Rathore", "Joshi", "Saxena", "Shukla", "Dubey", "Meena", "Jain",
             "Agrawal", "Srivastava", "Kushwaha", "Sahu", "Rajput", "Thakur", "Soni", "Bairwa",
             "Prajapati", "Choudhary", "Bhatt", "Trivedi", "Dwivedi", "Nayak", "Malviya")
make_name <- function(g) paste(if_else(g == "M", sample(male, length(g), TRUE),
                                       sample(female, length(g), TRUE)),
                               sample(surname, length(g), TRUE))
make_pan <- function(nm) paste0(map_chr(nm, \(x) paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = "")),
                                "P", str_sub(word(nm, -1), 1, 1),
                                sprintf("%04d", sample(1:9999, length(nm), TRUE)),
                                sample(LETTERS, length(nm), TRUE))
make_acct   <- function(n) sprintf("%011.0f", runif(n, 1e10, 9.99e10))
make_mobile <- function(n) paste0(sample(6:9, n, TRUE), sprintf("%09.0f", runif(n, 1e8, 9.99e8)))
retire_on <- function(dob) rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1))

# ---- Sanctioned strength ----
sanctioned <- expand_grid(office = offices$office, cadre = cadres$cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres, by = "cadre") |>
  mutate(sanctioned = if_else(office == "Head Office", ho, div)) |>
  filter(sanctioned > 0) |>
  select(office, cadre, sanctioned)

# ---- Staff on the rolls on 1 April 2024 ----
filled <- sanctioned |>
  mutate(vacant = rbinom(n(), sanctioned, 0.08),
         vacant = case_when(office == "Lakhanpur" & cadre == "Clerk" ~ 0L,
                            office == "Head Office" & cadre == "Assistant Engineer" ~ 0L,
                            office == "Amarpur" & cadre == "Junior Engineer" ~ pmax(vacant, 2L),
                            TRUE ~ vacant),
         n = sanctioned - vacant)
staff <- filled |>
  uncount(n) |>
  select(office, cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres |> select(cadre, level, min_pay, max_pay), by = "cadre")
n0 <- nrow(staff)
staff <- staff |>
  mutate(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), n0, TRUE, prob = c(0.72, 0.28)),
         dob = fy_start - round(runif(n0, 23, 59.9) * 365.25),
         doj = pmin(dob + round(runif(n0, 21, 33) * 365.25), fy_start - sample(30:500, n0, TRUE)),
         dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)
# Retirements in the year
r <- retire_on(staff$dob) <= fy_end
staff$dol[r] <- retire_on(staff$dob[r]); staff$leave_reason[r] <- "Retirement"
# Other leavers
others <- sample(which(!r & staff$office != "Lakhanpur"), 17)
staff$leave_reason[others] <- rep(c("Resignation", "Death", "Transfer out"), c(8, 3, 6))
staff$dol[others] <- fy_start + sample(20:340, 17)
# Planted. A clerk of Motinagar resigned on 31 August 2024 (paid two more months, below)
e_left <- sample(which(staff$office == "Motinagar" & staff$cadre == "Clerk" & is.na(staff$dol)), 1)
staff$dol[e_left] <- as.Date("2024-08-31"); staff$leave_reason[e_left] <- "Resignation"
# Planted. A senior clerk of Kesargaon reached 60 in August 2024; the master was never updated
e_super <- sample(which(staff$office == "Kesargaon" & staff$cadre == "Senior Clerk" & is.na(staff$dol)), 1)
staff$dob[e_super] <- as.Date("1964-08-20"); staff$doj[e_super] <- as.Date("1990-02-12")
staff$gender[e_super] <- "M"

# New joinees during the year, into vacant posts
vac <- filled |> filter(vacant > 0, !(office == "Head Office" & cadre == "Assistant Engineer"),
                        cadre %in% c("Junior Engineer", "Clerk", "Multi-tasking staff", "Gauge Reader",
                                     "Assistant Engineer"))
joiners <- vac |>
  slice_sample(n = 26, weight_by = vacant) |>
  select(office, cadre) |>
  left_join(cadres |> select(cadre, level, min_pay, max_pay), by = "cadre") |>
  mutate(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), n(), TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
         doj = fy_start + sample(10:330, n(), TRUE),
         dob = doj - round(runif(n(), 22, 30) * 365.25),
         dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)
# Planted. A Junior Engineer of Amarpur joined on 6 January 2025 (paid for December too, below)
joiners <- bind_rows(joiners, tibble(office = "Amarpur", cadre = "Junior Engineer", level = 6,
                                     min_pay = 35400, max_pay = 112400, gender = "M",
                                     doj = as.Date("2025-01-06"), dob = as.Date("1999-05-17"),
                                     dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_))
# One Assistant Engineer awaiting posting, held at Head Office
joiners <- bind_rows(joiners, tibble(office = "Head Office", cadre = "Assistant Engineer", level = 10,
                                     min_pay = 56100, max_pay = 177500, gender = "F",
                                     doj = as.Date("2024-09-16"), dob = as.Date("1996-02-03"),
                                     dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_))
# Planted. Three clerks of Lakhanpur who do not exist
ghosts <- tibble(office = "Lakhanpur", cadre = "Clerk", level = 2, min_pay = 19900, max_pay = 63200,
                 gender = c("M", "M", "F"),
                 doj = as.Date(c("2022-08-01", "2022-11-14", "2023-03-06")),
                 dob = as.Date(c("1993-04-11", "1995-09-23", "1996-12-02")),
                 dol = as.Date(NA), leave_reason = NA_character_)

emp <- bind_rows(staff, joiners, ghosts) |>
  mutate(emp_name = make_name(gender))
ne <- nrow(emp)
emp <- emp |>
  mutate(emp_code = sprintf("%06d", sample(1000:99999, ne)),
         pan = make_pan(emp_name),
         bank_account = make_acct(ne),
         mobile = make_mobile(ne),
         yrs = pmax(0, floor(as.numeric(fy_start - doj) / 365.25)),
         basic0 = pmin(round(min_pay * 1.03^yrs, -2), max_pay))
g_idx <- (ne - 2):ne
e_join <- which(emp$doj == as.Date("2025-01-06"))
emp$basic0[g_idx] <- c(21100, 20500, 20500)
# Ghosts share one mobile number, and the third is paid into a real clerk's account
emp$mobile[g_idx] <- "9812047736"
dealer <- sample(which(emp$office == "Lakhanpur" & emp$cadre == "Clerk" & is.na(emp$dol) &
                         emp$doj < as.Date("2020-01-01")), 1)
emp$bank_account[ne] <- emp$bank_account[dealer]
# Two married couples share a mobile number (innocent)
pool <- which(is.na(emp$dol) & !seq_len(ne) %in% c(g_idx, dealer))
cp <- c(rbind(sample(intersect(pool, which(emp$gender == "M")), 2),
              sample(intersect(pool, which(emp$gender == "F")), 2)))
emp$mobile[cp[c(2, 4)]] <- emp$mobile[cp[c(1, 3)]]
emp$emp_name[cp[c(2, 4)]] <- paste(word(emp$emp_name[cp[c(2, 4)]], 1, -2), word(emp$emp_name[cp[c(1, 3)]], -1))
# Two Junior Engineers on deputation to a project cell at Head Office, where there is no JE post
dep <- c(sample(which(emp$office == "Sonpur" & emp$cadre == "Junior Engineer" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1),
         sample(which(emp$office == "Dhaulagarh" & emp$cadre == "Junior Engineer" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1))
emp$office[dep] <- "Head Office"
# Planted. Two PANs in a wrong format, and one driver paid above the scale
bad_pan <- sample(which(is.na(emp$dol) & !seq_len(ne) %in% g_idx), 2)
emp$pan[bad_pan] <- c(str_sub(emp$pan[bad_pan[1]], 1, 9), str_replace(emp$pan[bad_pan[2]], "^(.{5})", "\\1O"))
emp$pan[bad_pan[2]] <- str_sub(emp$pan[bad_pan[2]], 1, 10)
e_scale <- sample(which(emp$office == "Head Office" & emp$cadre == "Driver" & is.na(emp$dol)), 1)
emp$basic0[e_scale] <- 66400

# ---- Change log of pay ----
inc <- emp |>
  mutate(i = row_number()) |>
  filter(doj <= as.Date("2024-01-01"), is.na(dol) | dol >= as.Date("2024-07-01")) |>
  transmute(i, type = "Increment", factor = 1.03, effective = as.Date("2024-07-01"),
            entered_on = as.Date("2024-07-01") + sample(1:12, n(), TRUE))
late_inc <- sample(setdiff(inc$i, c(g_idx, e_super)), 12)
inc$entered_on[inc$i %in% late_inc] <- as.Date("2024-10-01") + sample(2:20, 12, TRUE)
# Financial upgradations (MACP) for some, five of them entered late
macp_i <- sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < as.Date("2012-01-01")),
                         c(g_idx, late_inc, e_super, e_scale, dep)), 16)
macp <- tibble(i = macp_i, type = "Financial upgradation", factor = 1.05,
               effective = sample(seq(as.Date("2024-08-01"), by = "month", length.out = 6), 16, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(entered_on = effective + sample(3:15, 16, TRUE))
macp$effective[1:5] <- as.Date(c("2024-08-01", "2024-08-01", "2024-09-01", "2024-10-01", "2024-10-01"))
macp$entered_on[1:5] <- macp$effective[1:5] %m+% months(sample(2:3, 5, TRUE)) + sample(1:15, 5, TRUE)
e_dup_arr <- macp$i[1]
# Planted. An accountant of Chandanpur, upgradation from April entered only in January
e_bank <- sample(which(emp$office == "Chandanpur" & emp$cadre == "Accountant" & is.na(emp$dol) &
                         !seq_len(ne) %in% c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan)), 1)
macp <- bind_rows(macp, tibble(i = e_bank, type = "Financial upgradation", factor = 1.12,
                               effective = as.Date("2024-04-01"), entered_on = as.Date("2025-01-08")))
# Planted. A senior clerk of Belkheda given a second increment in January
e_twice <- sample(which(emp$office == "Belkheda" & emp$cadre == "Senior Clerk" &
                          seq_len(ne) %in% setdiff(inc$i, c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan))), 1)
# Planted. A clerk of Dhaulagarh whose pay was raised with no order
e_jump <- sample(which(emp$office == "Dhaulagarh" & emp$cadre == "Clerk" &
                         seq_len(ne) %in% setdiff(inc$i, c(late_inc, macp_i, bad_pan))), 1)
extra <- tibble(i = c(e_twice, e_jump), type = c("Increment", "Pay fixation"), factor = c(1.03, 1.22),
                effective = as.Date(c("2025-01-01", "2024-11-01")),
                entered_on = as.Date(c("2025-01-04", "2024-11-12")))
changes <- bind_rows(inc, macp, extra) |>
  mutate(paid_from = pmax(effective, floor_date(entered_on, "month")))

# Pay due and pay drawn, month by month
grid <- expand_grid(i = seq_len(ne), month = fy_months)
due_f <- grid |> left_join(changes, by = "i", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  summarise(f_due  = prod(if_else(!is.na(effective) & effective <= month, factor, 1)),
            f_paid = prod(if_else(!is.na(paid_from) & paid_from <= month, factor, 1)),
            .by = c(i, month))
da_rate <- function(m) if_else(m >= as.Date("2024-10-01"), 0.53, 0.50)
pay_grid <- due_f |>
  mutate(basic_due  = round(emp$basic0[i] * f_due, -2),
         basic_paid = round(emp$basic0[i] * f_paid, -2))

# Log entries, with values before and after
changes <- changes |>
  mutate(new_value = pay_grid$basic_due[match(paste(i, effective), paste(pay_grid$i, pay_grid$month))],
         old_value = if_else(effective == fy_start, emp$basic0[i] / factor,
                             pay_grid$basic_due[match(paste(i, effective %m-% months(1)),
                                                      paste(pay_grid$i, pay_grid$month))]),
         old_value = round(old_value, -2))
seq_ref <- function(prefix, n) sprintf("%s/24-25/%04d", prefix, sample(1:9999, n))
pay_log <- changes |>
  mutate(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], field = "basic_pay",
         order_ref = case_when(type == "Increment" ~ seq_ref("INC", n()),
                               type == "Financial upgradation" ~ seq_ref("MACP", n()),
                               TRUE ~ NA_character_),
         entered_by = if_else(i == e_jump, "DEO-07",
                              sample(sprintf("DEO-%02d", 1:6), n(), TRUE)))

# ---- Arrears ----
arr <- pay_grid |>
  filter(basic_due > basic_paid) |>
  inner_join(changes |> filter(paid_from > effective) |> select(i, type, entered_on), by = "i") |>
  summarise(period_from = min(month), period_to = max(month),
            amount = round(sum((basic_due - basic_paid) * (1 + da_rate(month)))),
            .by = c(i, type, entered_on)) |>
  mutate(arrear_type = paste(type, "arrears"),
         paid_on = entered_on + sample(6:12, n(), TRUE))
arr$paid_on[arr$i == e_bank] <- as.Date("2025-01-17")
# Planted. One arrears bill paid twice
dup_row <- arr |> filter(i == e_dup_arr) |> mutate(paid_on = paid_on + 56)
arr <- bind_rows(arr, dup_row)
# Genuine arrears of transport allowance after a late order for drivers (innocent noise)
ta_arr <- tibble(i = which(emp$cadre == "Driver" & is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < fy_start),
                 type = "x", entered_on = as.Date("2024-12-10"), period_from = as.Date("2024-04-01"),
                 period_to = as.Date("2024-11-01"), amount = 8 * 600,
                 arrear_type = "Transport allowance arrears", paid_on = as.Date("2024-12-18"))
arr <- bind_rows(arr, ta_arr) |>
  filter(paid_on <= fy_end) |>
  arrange(paid_on, i)

# ---- Bank account changes ----
bchg <- tibble(i = sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol)), c(g_idx, dealer, e_bank)), 22),
               changed_on = fy_start + sample(5:350, 22, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(new_value = make_acct(n()))
# Planted. The Chandanpur accountant's account changed four days before the arrears, and back after
temp_acct <- make_acct(1)
bchg <- bind_rows(bchg, tibble(i = e_bank, changed_on = as.Date(c("2025-01-13", "2025-01-27")),
                               new_value = c(temp_acct, emp$bank_account[e_bank])))
bchg <- bchg |> arrange(i, changed_on) |>
  mutate(old_value = lag(new_value, default = NA), .by = i) |>
  mutate(old_value = coalesce(old_value, emp$bank_account[i]))
acct_on <- function(k, d) {
  map2_chr(k, d, \(kk, dd) {
    ch <- bchg[bchg$i == kk & bchg$changed_on <= dd, ]
    if (nrow(ch) == 0) emp$bank_account[kk] else ch$new_value[nrow(ch)]
  })
}
emp_final_acct <- acct_on(seq_len(ne), fy_end)
arr <- arr |> mutate(paid_to_account = acct_on(i, paid_on))

# ---- Monthly payroll ----
hra_rate <- c(X = 0.30, Y = 0.20, Z = 0.10)
on_roll <- grid |>
  mutate(m_end = month_end(month), start = emp$doj[i], stop = coalesce(emp$dol[i], fy_end),
         days = as.numeric(pmin(m_end, stop) - pmax(month, start)) + 1,
         frac = pmin(1, days / as.numeric(m_end - month + 1))) |>
  filter(days > 0)
# Planted. Paid after leaving (Motinagar) and before joining (Amarpur)
on_roll <- bind_rows(on_roll,
                     tibble(i = e_left, month = as.Date(c("2024-09-01", "2024-10-01")), frac = 1),
                     tibble(i = e_join, month = as.Date("2024-12-01"), frac = 1))
# The Kesargaon senior clerk stays on the rolls all year (no date of leaving in the master)
payroll <- on_roll |>
  select(i, month, frac) |>
  left_join(pay_grid |> select(i, month, basic_paid), by = c("i", "month")) |>
  mutate(office = emp$office[i], level = emp$level[i],
         city_class = offices$city_class[match(office, offices$office)],
         days_paid = round(frac * days_in_month(month)),
         basic_pay = round(basic_paid * frac),
         da_pct = da_rate(month),
         # Planted. Sonpur pays the new DA rate two months early
         da_pct = if_else(office == "Sonpur" & month %in% as.Date(c("2024-08-01", "2024-09-01")), 0.53, da_pct),
         da = round(da_pct * basic_pay),
         hra = round(hra_rate[city_class] * basic_pay),
         other_allow = round(case_when(level >= 9 ~ 7200, level >= 3 ~ 3600, TRUE ~ 1800) * frac),
         gross = basic_pay + da + hra + other_allow,
         deductions = round(0.10 * (basic_pay + da)) + 200 + round(pmax(0, gross - 90000) * 0.10),
         net_pay = gross - deductions,
         pay_date = month_end(month),
         bank_account = acct_on(i, pay_date),
         emp_code = emp$emp_code[i])
# Planted. A person not in the master, paid by Belkheda from January
stranger <- payroll |> filter(office == "Belkheda", level == 1, month >= as.Date("2025-01-01")) |>
  filter(i == i[1]) |>
  mutate(emp_code = "070815", bank_account = make_acct(1))
# Planted. One January salary at Sonpur paid twice
dup_sal <- payroll |> filter(office == "Sonpur", month == as.Date("2025-01-01")) |> slice_sample(n = 1)
payroll <- bind_rows(payroll, stranger, dup_sal) |>
  arrange(month, office, emp_code) |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, days_paid, basic_pay, da, hra, other_allow, gross, deductions, net_pay,
         pay_date, bank_account)

# ---- Attendance summary ----
long_leave <- tibble(i = sample(setdiff(which(is.na(emp$dol) & emp$doj < fy_start),
                                        c(g_idx, dealer, e_super, e_bank, e_jump, e_twice, e_scale, e_left,
                                          bad_pan, cp, dep, e_dup_arr, late_inc)), 5),
                     from = sample(fy_months[2:7], 5, TRUE), len = sample(3:5, 5, TRUE))
attendance <- on_roll |>
  filter(!i %in% g_idx,
         !(i == e_left & month > as.Date("2024-08-01")),
         !(i == e_join & month < as.Date("2025-01-01")),
         !(i == e_super & month > as.Date("2024-08-01"))) |>
  left_join(long_leave, by = "i") |>
  filter(is.na(from) | month < from | month >= from %m+% months(len)) |>
  mutate(working = 26 - (wday(month_end(month)) == 1),
         days_leave = sample(0:3, n(), TRUE, prob = c(5, 3, 2, 1)),
         days_present = pmax(0, round(working * frac) - days_leave),
         emp_code = as.numeric(emp$emp_code[i])) |>
  select(emp_code, month, days_present, days_leave)

# ---- Employee master, at 31 March 2025 ----
employees <- emp |>
  mutate(bank_account = emp_final_acct) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, gender, cadre, office, dob, doj, dol, leave_reason, pan, bank_account, mobile) |>
  arrange(emp_code)
master_changes <- bind_rows(
  pay_log |> transmute(emp_code, field, change_type = type, old_value = as.character(old_value),
                       new_value = as.character(new_value), effective_from = effective,
                       order_ref, entered_on, entered_by),
  bchg |> transmute(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], field = "bank_account", change_type = "Bank details",
                    old_value, new_value, effective_from = changed_on,
                    order_ref = NA_character_, entered_on = changed_on,
                    entered_by = if_else(i == e_bank, "DEO-03", sample(sprintf("DEO-%02d", 1:6), n(), TRUE)))
) |> arrange(entered_on, emp_code)
arrears <- arr |>
  mutate(emp_code = emp$emp_code[i], bill_no = sprintf("SB/%04d", sample(1000:9999, n()))) |>
  select(emp_code, arrear_type, period_from, period_to, amount, bill_no, paid_on, paid_to_account)

bank_salary <- bind_rows(payroll |> transmute(month = floor_date(pay_date, "month"), amount = net_pay),
                         arrears |> transmute(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), amount)) |>
  summarise(bank_debits = sum(amount), .by = month) |> arrange(month)

# ---- Pensions ----
np <- 1250
pen <- tibble(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), np, TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2)),
              age = 60.1 + 38 * rbeta(np, 1, 2.6)) |>
  mutate(dob = fy_start - round(age * 365.25))
# Genuine pensioners over 100, and one planted
pen <- bind_rows(pen, tibble(gender = c("M", "F", "M", "M", "M"),
                             dob = as.Date(c("1922-08-14", "1923-01-30", "1924-02-19", "1921-11-05",
                                             "1920-06-14"))))
np <- nrow(pen)
pen <- pen |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender), pension_type = "Service", linked_ppo = NA_character_,
         retirement_date = retire_on(dob), pension_start = retirement_date + 1,
         last_pay = round(sample(c(18000, 19900, 25500, 35400, 56100, 67700), np, TRUE,
                                 prob = c(5, 6, 4, 4, 2, 1)) * runif(np, 1.2, 2.3), -2),
         share = if_else(runif(np) < 0.06, runif(np, 0.30, 0.48), 0.5),
         monthly_pension = pmax(round(share * last_pay), 9000))
# New pensioners, the employees who retired during the year
newp <- emp |>
  mutate(i = row_number()) |>
  filter(leave_reason %in% "Retirement") |>
  left_join(pay_grid |> filter(month == as.Date("2025-03-01")) |> select(i, basic_due), by = "i") |>
  transmute(gender, dob, name = emp_name, pension_type = "Service", linked_ppo = NA_character_,
            retirement_date = dol, pension_start = dol + 1, last_pay = basic_due, share = 0.5,
            monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.5 * last_pay), 9000)) |>
  filter(pension_start <= fy_end)
pen <- bind_rows(pen, newp)
# Existing family pensioners
nf <- 290
famold <- tibble(gender = sample(c("F", "M"), nf, TRUE, prob = c(0.92, 0.08)),
                 dob = fy_start - round(runif(nf, 52, 94) * 365.25)) |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender), pension_type = "Family",
         linked_ppo = if_else(runif(nf) < 0.7, sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(1:8000, nf)), NA_character_),
         retirement_date = as.Date(NA),
         pension_start = fy_start - sample(200:9000, nf, TRUE),
         last_pay = round(sample(c(18000, 19900, 25500, 35400, 56100), nf, TRUE) * runif(nf, 1.2, 2.2), -2),
         share = 0.3, monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.3 * last_pay), 9000))
pen <- bind_rows(pen, famold) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(8001:29999, n())),
         date_of_death = as.Date(NA))
# Planted. One pension far above the rule
p_high <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$share == 0.5 & pen$last_pay > 60000 &
                         pen$pension_start < fy_start), 1)
pen$monthly_pension[p_high] <- round(0.78 * pen$last_pay[p_high])
p_old <- which(pen$dob == as.Date("1920-06-14"))
# Deaths of pensioners in the year. Most leave a spouse, who gets a family pension
dead <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$pension_start < fy_start &
                       pen$dob > as.Date("1925-01-01") & seq_len(nrow(pen)) != p_high), 14,
               prob = as.numeric(fy_start - pen$dob[pen$pension_type == "Service" & pen$pension_start < fy_start &
                                                     pen$dob > as.Date("1925-01-01") &
                                                     seq_len(nrow(pen)) != p_high])^3)
pen$date_of_death[dead] <- fy_start + sample(10:300, 14)
dm <- dead[pen$gender[dead] == "M"][1]
dead <- c(dm, setdiff(dead, dm))
p_both <- dead[1]
pen$date_of_death[p_both] <- as.Date("2024-07-19")
spouse <- pen[dead[1:9], ] |>
  transmute(gender = if_else(gender == "M", "F", "M"),
            dob = dob + round(runif(9, 2, 7) * 365.25),
            name = paste(if_else(gender == "F", sample(female, 9, TRUE), sample(male, 9, TRUE)), word(name, -1)),
            pension_type = "Family", linked_ppo = ppo_no, retirement_date = as.Date(NA),
            pension_start = floor_date(date_of_death, "month") %m+% months(1),
            last_pay, share = 0.3, monthly_pension = pmax(round(0.3 * last_pay), 9000),
            ppo_no = sprintf("PPO/%05d", sample(30001:30999, 9)), date_of_death = as.Date(NA))
pen <- bind_rows(pen, spouse) |>
  mutate(bank_account = make_acct(n()))
nP <- nrow(pen)

# Monthly pension payments
pension_paid <- expand_grid(k = seq_len(nP), month = fy_months) |>
  filter(pen$pension_start[k] <= month_end(month),
         is.na(pen$date_of_death[k]) | month <= floor_date(pen$date_of_death[k], "month") |
           k == p_both) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = pen$ppo_no[k], amount = pen$monthly_pension[k], paid_on = month_end(month)) |>
  select(ppo_no, month, paid_on, amount)

# Commutation for the new pensioners, paid once each, and once twice (planted)
commutation <- pen |>
  filter(pension_type == "Service", pension_start >= fy_start) |>
  transmute(ppo_no, paid_on = pension_start + sample(30:75, n(), TRUE),
            amount = round(0.4 * monthly_pension * 12 * 8.194)) |>
  filter(paid_on <= fy_end)
p_comm <- commutation$ppo_no[2]
commutation <- bind_rows(commutation,
                         commutation |> filter(ppo_no == p_comm) |> mutate(paid_on = paid_on + 97)) |>
  arrange(paid_on) |>
  mutate(bill_no = sprintf("CB/%04d", sample(1000:9999, n())))

# Life certificates
lc <- pen |> mutate(k = row_number()) |>
  filter(pension_start < as.Date("2024-11-01"))
cert_day <- function(n, yr) as.Date(paste0(yr, "-11-01")) + round(rnorm(n, 12, 9))
life_certs <- bind_rows(
  lc |> filter(pension_start < as.Date("2023-11-01")) |> transmute(k, cert_date = cert_day(n(), 2023)),
  lc |> transmute(k, cert_date = cert_day(n(), 2024))
) |>
  filter(is.na(pen$date_of_death[k]) | cert_date < pen$date_of_death[k])
# Late certificates (innocent but a lapse): the 2024 certificate came in January or February
late_lc <- sample(setdiff(lc$k[lc$pension_start < as.Date("2023-06-01") & is.na(pen$date_of_death[lc$k])],
                          c(p_old, p_high)), 11)
life_certs <- life_certs |>
  mutate(cert_date = if_else(k %in% late_lc & cert_date >= as.Date("2024-09-01"),
                             as.Date("2025-01-04") + sample(0:50, n(), TRUE), cert_date),
         cert_date = if_else(k %in% late_lc & cert_date < as.Date("2024-01-01"),
                             as.Date("2023-11-01") + sample(0:6, n(), TRUE), cert_date))
# Planted. The oldest pensioner's last certificate is from November 2021
life_certs <- life_certs |> filter(k != p_old) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(k = p_old, cert_date = as.Date("2021-11-18"))) |>
  mutate(ppo_no = pen$ppo_no[k]) |>
  arrange(ppo_no, cert_date) |>
  select(ppo_no, cert_date)

pensioners <- pen |>
  select(ppo_no, name, gender, dob, pension_type, linked_ppo, retirement_date, pension_start,
         last_pay, monthly_pension, date_of_death, bank_account) |>
  arrange(ppo_no)
treasury_pension <- bind_rows(pension_paid |> select(month, amount),
                              commutation |> transmute(month = floor_date(paid_on, "month"), amount)) |>
  summarise(treasury_debits = sum(amount), .by = month) |> arrange(month)

# ---- Old age pension list of the welfare department ----
no <- 900
oap <- tibble(gender = sample(c("M", "F"), no, TRUE),
              dob = fy_start - round(runif(no, 60, 92) * 365.25)) |>
  mutate(name = make_name(gender))
# Planted. Two service pensioners also on the old age pension list, names written differently
twins <- sample(which(pen$pension_type == "Service" & is.na(pen$date_of_death) & pen$gender == "M" &
                        pen$pension_start < fy_start & seq_len(nP) != p_old), 2)
oap <- bind_rows(oap, tibble(gender = "M", dob = pen$dob[twins],
                             name = c(str_replace(pen$name[twins[1]], "(\\w+) (\\w+)$", "\\1 Kumar \\2"),
                                      str_replace_all(pen$name[twins[2]], c("ee" = "i", "sh" = "s", "v" = "w")))))
oap <- oap |>
  slice_sample(prop = 1) |>
  mutate(oap_id = sprintf("OAP-%04d", row_number()),
         district = sample(c("North", "South", "East", "West"), n(), TRUE),
         monthly_pension = 1000) |>
  select(oap_id, name, gender, dob, district, monthly_pension)
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("employees", "master_changes", "payroll", "arrears", "sanctioned",
                          "attendance", "pensioners", "pension_paid", "life_certs", "commutation",
                          "bank_salary", "treasury_pension", "oap")))

Two keys link the tables. emp_code links the employee master to the change log, payroll, arrears and attendance. ppo_no links the pension master to the payments, certificates and commutation. Every test below is a join along one of these links.






TipAudit tip, the data to request



Ask for the whole year, in raw form. For pay, that is the employee master with its change log, the monthly payroll with the account credited, the arrears bills, the sanctioned strength and the attendance summary. For pensions, it is the pension master, the monthly payments, the life certificate register and the commutation payments. The change log matters most. The current master shows only the last value, and hides a change made and then reversed. Ask also for the bank’s and treasury’s monthly totals. Note who ran each extract and when.

7.6 Payroll against attendance
A real employee leaves a trail of attendance and leave. A ghost leaves only a salary. So an employee paid for a month with no attendance record at all needs a look. Let us join the payroll with the attendance summary.

glimpse(attendance)

Rows: 10,759
Columns: 4
$ emp_code     <dbl> 13789, 13789, 13789, 13789, 13789, 13789, 13789, 13789, 1…
$ month        <date> 2024-04-01, 2024-05-01, 2024-06-01, 2024-07-01, 2024-08-…
$ days_present <dbl> 25, 26, 25, 26, 25, 26, 25, 26, 24, 25, 23, 23, 25, 26, 2…
$ days_leave   <int> 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0, 1, 2, …

payroll |>
  semi_join(attendance |> mutate(emp_code = as.character(emp_code)), by = "emp_code") |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


No row matches. The glimpse() shows why. The attendance file stores the employee code as a number, so the code 013789 became 13789. This is the problem of lost leading zeros of Section 20.19. We pad the codes back to six digits with str_pad().

attendance <- attendance |>
  mutate(emp_code = str_pad(as.character(emp_code), width = 6, pad = "0"))

Now the months paid with no attendance record at all.

no_record <- payroll |>
  anti_join(attendance, by = c("emp_code", "month")) |>
  summarise(months_no_record = n_distinct(month), .by = c(emp_code, office)) |>
  left_join(payroll |> summarise(months_paid = n_distinct(month), .by = emp_code), by = "emp_code") |>
  left_join(employees |> select(emp_code, cadre, mobile), by = "emp_code") |>
  arrange(desc(months_no_record))

12 codes were paid for at least one month with no record. They fall into three groups.


No record in any month. Three clerks of Lakhanpur were paid in all 12 months and never marked present or on leave. They share one mobile number. With them is the code 070815, which is not in the master at all.

A few months with no record, explained by our other tests. The clerk paid after resigning and the engineer paid before joining appear for those months. A senior clerk of Kesargaon, 099726, has no record for 7 months. We see why in Section 7.8.

A few months with no record, and nothing else wrong. Five employees have runs of 3 to 5 months with no record, in the middle of the year. This is the pattern of long leave sanctioned by a higher office and never entered in the attendance system. The leave orders will show.


f_noatt_all <- all_months$emp_code
f_noatt_some <- some_months$emp_code







WarningCaution, many flags have innocent causes



A missing attendance record may mean long leave, deputation, training or a late entry. A pay rise without an order may be an order not yet entered. A count above the posts may be an officer awaiting posting. So treat every flag as a question to the office. Ask for the leave, deputation or relieving order before calling anything an irregularity. An office that cannot produce the papers for many flags has a weak control, even when no money is lost.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
text:
7.7 Pensions
Pensions are paid for decades, often by a treasury or a bank, and nobody sees the pensioner each month. The main control is the yearly life certificate, by which the pensioner proves that he or she is alive. When it fails, a pension may run on long after death.

pensioners |>
  count(pension_type)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  pension_type     n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Family         299
2 Service       1273



7.7.1 Pensioners of a great age
A pensioner over 100 is rare but possible. Such a pensioner should have a recent life certificate. Let us find the living pensioners aged 100 or more on 31 March 2025, with their latest certificate. interval() and time_length() give the age in completed years, as in Chapter 18.

last_cert <- life_certs |>
  summarise(last_cert = max(cert_date), .by = ppo_no)

very_old <- pensioners |>
  filter(is.na(date_of_death)) |>
  mutate(age = floor(time_length(interval(dob, as.Date("2025-03-31")), "years"))) |>
  filter(age >= 100) |>
  left_join(last_cert, by = "ppo_no")
very_old |>
  select(ppo_no, name, age, pension_type, monthly_pension, last_cert)

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  ppo_no    name                  age pension_type monthly_pension last_cert 
  <chr>     <chr>               <dbl> <chr>                  <dbl> <date>    
1 PPO/13520 Mahesh Mishra         101 Service                34950 2024-10-23
2 PPO/21070 Kavita Verma          102 Service                17650 2024-11-06
3 PPO/25333 Satish Joshi          103 Service                16550 2024-10-31
4 PPO/27324 Rajendra Srivastava   104 Service                16300 2021-11-18
5 PPO/28677 Govind Sahu           102 Service                17650 2024-11-13


Five living pensioners are 100 or older. Four of them sent a life certificate in October 2024 or November 2024, and are simply very old. One is different. Rajendra Srivastava, PPO/27324, is 104 years old, and his last life certificate is dated 18 November 2021.

f_old <- old_bad$ppo_no


7.7.2 Pension paid after the life certificate expired
Let us test every payment. In our example norm, a life certificate is valid until the end of the same month a year later. A new pensioner needs none in the first year, so the start of the pension also counts as a check. For each payment we need the latest check on or before it. This is a rolling join with closest(), as for the rate in force in Section 16.6.

checks <- bind_rows(life_certs,
                    pensioners |> transmute(ppo_no, cert_date = pension_start))

expired <- pension_paid |>
  left_join(checks, by = join_by(ppo_no, closest(paid_on >= cert_date))) |>
  mutate(valid_till = rollforward(cert_date %m+% years(1))) |>
  filter(paid_on > valid_till)

expired_by_ppo <- expired |>
  summarise(months = n(), amount = sum(amount), last_check = max(cert_date), .by = ppo_no) |>
  arrange(desc(months))
expired_by_ppo

# A tibble: 15 × 4
   ppo_no    months amount last_check
   <chr>      <int>  <dbl> <date>    
 1 PPO/27324     12 195600 2021-11-18
 2 PPO/13789      4  77800 2023-11-16
 3 PPO/27749      2  39900 2023-11-01
 4 PPO/19700      2  36200 2023-11-04
 5 PPO/21380      2  36800 2023-11-02
 6 PPO/21087      2  41900 2023-11-04
 7 PPO/09624      2  56100 2023-11-05
 8 PPO/13121      2  30300 2023-11-07
 9 PPO/28305      1  18400 2023-10-31
10 PPO/22377      1  54700 2023-10-31
11 PPO/15280      1  19450 2023-11-06
12 PPO/19184      1  13800 2023-11-06
13 PPO/20853      1  36450 2023-11-03
14 PPO/19503      1  19350 2023-11-04
15 PPO/28762      1  30450 2023-11-07


rollforward() moves a date to the end of its month. 15 pensioners were paid at least once on an expired certificate. The planted pensioner over 100 heads the list, with all 12 months of the year, ₹2 lakh. The next, PPO/13789, was paid for 4 months on an expired certificate. That pensioner died in July 2024, so no new certificate could come. We meet him again in the next section. The other 13 were paid for 1 or 2 months each. Their new certificates came in later, between 4 December 2024 and 23 February 2025. The pensioners were alive, but the payments were made without the check. That lapse is worth reporting as a pattern.

f_expired <- expired_by_ppo$ppo_no


7.7.3 Family pension and service pension together
When a pensioner dies, the pension stops, and the spouse may get a family pension from the next month. The two should never be paid for the same month. We join each family pension to the payments of its linked_ppo from the month it started.

both_paid <- pensioners |>
  filter(pension_type == "Family", !is.na(linked_ppo)) |>
  select(family_ppo = ppo_no, linked_ppo, family_start = pension_start) |>
  inner_join(pension_paid, by = join_by(linked_ppo == ppo_no, family_start <= month))

both_paid |>
  summarise(months = n(), amount = sum(amount), from = min(month), to = max(month),
            .by = c(family_ppo, linked_ppo))

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  family_ppo linked_ppo months amount from       to        
  <chr>      <chr>       <int>  <dbl> <date>     <date>    
1 PPO/30941  PPO/13789       8 155600 2024-08-01 2025-03-01


Of the 9 family pensions that began during the year, one overlaps. Lalit Srivastava, PPO/13789, died on 19 July 2024. His widow’s family pension, PPO/30941, began in August 2024, yet his own pension was paid every month from August 2024 to March 2025, ₹1.6 lakh. The office that sanctioned the family pension knew of the death, but the service pension was never stopped. A simpler test needs no family pension. Any payment for a month after a recorded death is wrong.

pension_paid |>
  inner_join(pensioners |> filter(!is.na(date_of_death)) |> select(ppo_no, date_of_death), by = "ppo_no") |>
  filter(month > floor_date(date_of_death, "month")) |>
  count(ppo_no, date_of_death, name = "months_after_death")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  ppo_no    date_of_death months_after_death
  <chr>     <date>                     <int>
1 PPO/13789 2024-07-19                     8


The same pensioner appears. Where a death is not recorded at all, link the list with the death register, as Chapter 36 did.

f_both <- unique(c(bp$family_ppo, bp$linked_ppo))


7.7.4 Commutation paid twice
On retirement, a pensioner may commute part of the pension, taking a lump sum once in return for a smaller pension for some years. Our monthly payments leave out the reduction, for simplicity. Let us look for a PPO paid more than once.

commutation |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = ppo_no)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  ppo_no    paid_on    amount bill_no
  <chr>     <date>      <dbl> <chr>  
1 PPO/26549 2024-11-27 940016 CB/7241
2 PPO/26549 2025-03-04 940016 CB/7595


Bharat Choudhary, PPO/26549, was paid a commutation of ₹9.4 lakh on 27 November 2024, and again on 4 March 2025, by a different bill. Of 14 commutations paid in the year, this is the only repeat. It is also the largest single overpayment in this chapter.

f_comm <- unique(cm$ppo_no)


7.7.5 Pension against a simple rule
A pension depends on the last pay and the length of service, under detailed rules that the auditor should apply as they stand. For a first screen, a simple rule shows the cases far off the mark. Our illustrative rule is the one stated with the data. A pension below it may be correct, since short service gives less. A pension well above it needs a look.

pension_rule <- pensioners |>
  mutate(rule_share = if_else(pension_type == "Service", 0.5, 0.3),
         by_rule = pmax(round(rule_share * last_pay), 9000),
         ratio = round(monthly_pension / by_rule, 2))

pension_rule |>
  count(above = ratio > 1.05, below = ratio < 0.95)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  above below     n
  <lgl> <lgl> <int>
1 FALSE FALSE  1503
2 FALSE TRUE     68
3 TRUE  FALSE     1

pension_rule |>
  filter(ratio > 1.05) |>
  select(ppo_no, name, pension_type, last_pay, monthly_pension, by_rule, ratio)

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  ppo_no    name         pension_type last_pay monthly_pension by_rule ratio
  <chr>     <chr>        <chr>           <dbl>           <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 PPO/16475 Jagdish Sahu Service        143600          112008   71800  1.56


68 pensions are below the rule, which short service explains. One is above it. Jagdish Sahu, PPO/16475, draws ₹1,12,008 a month, against ₹71,800 by the rule, 1.56 times as much. If the rule holds, the excess for this year alone is ₹4.8 lakh. A pension fixed wrongly is paid wrongly for life. Ask for the pension papers and work it out under the real rules.

f_rule <- hi$ppo_no


7.7.6 The same person on two pension lists
Under many schemes, a service pensioner may not also draw an old age pension, as in Section 9.2. The two lists have no common key, so we link them as in Chapter 36. We block on date of birth and gender, and compare names with the Jaro-Winkler distance of Chapter 35.

std_name <- function(x) str_squish(str_to_lower(str_remove_all(x, "[^A-Za-z ]")))

candidates <- pensioners |>
  filter(pension_type == "Service", is.na(date_of_death)) |>
  select(ppo_no, name, gender, dob) |>
  inner_join(oap |> select(oap_id, oap_name = name, gender, dob), by = c("gender", "dob"),
             relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(jw = round(stringdist(std_name(name), std_name(oap_name), method = "jw", p = 0.1), 3)) |>
  arrange(jw)
nrow(candidates)

[1] 62

head(candidates, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  ppo_no    name            gender dob        oap_id   oap_name              jw
  <chr>     <chr>           <chr>  <date>     <chr>    <chr>              <dbl>
1 PPO/16221 Girish Bhatt    M      1937-07-28 OAP-0406 Girish Kumar Bhatt 0.092
2 PPO/13657 Praveen Nayak   M      1959-06-29 OAP-0727 Prawin Nayak       0.093
3 PPO/16115 Rajendra Saxena M      1951-09-10 OAP-0599 Rakesh Chauhan     0.272
4 PPO/10627 Shyam Sahu      M      1947-03-03 OAP-0017 Satish Mishra      0.288
5 PPO/14039 Anil Kushwaha   M      1951-01-15 OAP-0504 Kailash Agrawal    0.305


A person on one list may share a date of birth with several on the other, so we tell inner_join() to expect a many-to-many relationship. 62 pairs share a date of birth and gender. Two pairs have very close names, Girish Bhatt and Girish Kumar Bhatt, and Praveen Nayak and Prawin Nayak, with distances of 0.092 and 0.093. The next pair, Rajendra Saxena and Rakesh Chauhan, is plainly two different people, at 0.272. A gap like this makes the cut-off easy, here 0.15. The close pairs are candidates, not findings. The welfare department should check them against its own papers before stopping either pension.

f_twolists <- twin$ppo_no







WarningCaution, privacy of employee and pensioner data



Payroll and pension data hold names, dates of birth, PANs, bank accounts and mobile numbers of thousands of people. Use them only for the audit, keep them in a protected folder, and do not put full account numbers or PANs in the report. Use the employee codes and PPO numbers instead. Linking with another department’s list needs particular care. Chapter 9 explains how to mask, pseudonymise and match lists without sharing identifiers. A name in a list of flags is not a finding against that person.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
text:
7.8 What earlier chapters add
Several tests from earlier chapters apply directly. We run each in a few lines, and the chapters cited explain them in full.
The pay bill rule book, Chapter 31. We check three rules with filter(), as in Section 31.2. The first is DA at the rate in force. A rolling join finds the rate for each month, as in Section 16.5 and Section 16.6.

da_rates <- tibble(effective_from = as.Date(c("2024-01-01", "2024-10-01")),
                   da_pct = c(50, 53))

da_wrong <- payroll |>
  left_join(da_rates, by = join_by(closest(month >= effective_from))) |>
  filter(abs(da - da_pct / 100 * basic_pay) > 1)
da_wrong |>
  summarise(employees = n(), excess = sum(da - round(da_pct / 100 * basic_pay)), .by = c(office, month))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  office month      employees excess
  <chr>  <date>         <int>  <dbl>
1 Sonpur 2024-08-01       101 122343
2 Sonpur 2024-09-01       101 122059


Sonpur paid DA at the new rate of 53% in August and September, before it took effect, an excess of ₹2.4 lakh. This is an office-wide error, noted against the office. Next come basic pay within the range of the cadre, with example ranges, and the PAN format of Section 21.10.

pay_range <- tribble(
  ~cadre,                ~min_pay, ~max_pay,
  "Executive Engineer",  67700,    208700,
  "Assistant Engineer",  56100,    177500,
  "Junior Engineer",     35400,    112400,
  "Accountant",          35400,    112400,
  "Senior Clerk",        25500,     81100,
  "Clerk",               19900,     63200,
  "Driver",              19900,     63200,
  "Multi-tasking staff", 18000,     56900,
  "Gauge Reader",        18000,     56900)

out_of_range <- payroll |>
  filter(days_paid == days_in_month(month)) |>
  inner_join(employees |> select(emp_code, cadre), by = "emp_code") |>
  left_join(pay_range, by = "cadre") |>
  filter(basic_pay < min_pay | basic_pay > max_pay)
out_of_range |>
  summarise(months = n(), basic_pay = max(basic_pay), max_pay = max(max_pay), .by = c(emp_code, cadre))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  emp_code cadre  months basic_pay max_pay
  <chr>    <chr>   <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 090625   Driver     12     68400   63200

bad_pan <- employees |>
  filter(!str_detect(pan, "^[A-Z]{3}P[A-Z][0-9]{4}[A-Z]$"))
bad_pan |>
  select(emp_code, office, pan)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  emp_code office      pan       
  <chr>    <chr>       <chr>     
1 083465   Head Office FKBPMO1484
2 089995   Lakhanpur   YDZPJ9738 


A driver, 090625, is paid above the top of the driver’s range in all 12 months. Two PANs are in a wrong format. One is too short, and one has the letter O where a digit should be. The HRA rule passes for every row, as an exercise shows.
Superannuation, Chapter 18 and Section 31.3. An employee retires at the end of the month of reaching 60. A person reaches an age on the day before the birthday, so we subtract a day before rolling forward to the month end.

past_60 <- employees |>
  mutate(superannuation = rollforward(dob %m+% years(60) - days(1))) |>
  filter(superannuation <= as.Date("2025-03-31"), is.na(dol) | dol > superannuation)
past_60 |>
  select(emp_code, office, cadre, dob, superannuation, dol)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  emp_code office    cadre        dob        superannuation dol   
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>        <date>     <date>         <date>
1 099726   Kesargaon Senior Clerk 1964-08-20 2024-08-31     NA    


The 20 employees who retired during the year all left on the right date. One did not leave at all. Employee 099726, a senior clerk of Kesargaon, was born on 20 August 1964 and should have retired on 31 August 2024. The master has no date of leaving, and the payroll paid ₹7.4 lakh for the 7 months after. That is why the code had no attendance after August. Perhaps he was re-employed, which needs an order. Perhaps he simply went home.
Employees not in the master. The code 070815 found in Section 7.3 was paid ₹1,05,828 by Belkheda in three months, and has no attendance either. A payroll that accepts such a code has lost its main control.
One account, several salaries, Section 19.4.

shared_acct <- payroll |>
  summarise(employees = n_distinct(emp_code), codes = paste(sort(unique(emp_code)), collapse = ", "),
            .by = c(bank_account, month)) |>
  filter(employees > 1) |>
  count(codes, name = "months")
shared_acct

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  codes          months
  <chr>           <int>
1 044813, 062156     12


One account received two salaries in every month of the year. One of the two codes is 062156, a Lakhanpur clerk with no attendance. The other is 044813, Ram Kishore Jain, also a clerk of Lakhanpur, who attends every month. We follow this in Section 7.10.
The same salary paid twice, Section 34.4.

dup_salary <- payroll |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(emp_code, month))
dup_salary |>
  select(emp_code, office, month, net_pay, bank_account)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  emp_code office month      net_pay bank_account
  <chr>    <chr>  <date>       <dbl> <chr>       
1 028813   Sonpur 2025-01-01   62695 95575342515 
2 028813   Sonpur 2025-01-01   62695 95575342515 


Employee 028813 of Sonpur was paid the salary of January 2025 twice, ₹62,695 each time. Both reached the bank, so the completeness check could not see it.
Ghost employees by regression, Section 40.9. That section found offices that spent more on salary than their staff explained. With only nine offices, a regression has too few points. The tests against posts and attendance do the job person by person.
Other chapters. The ledger entries for salaries and pensions can be tested as in Chapter 1. Each salary credit can be matched with the bank item by item, as in Chapter 2. A pension list is checked against a death register in Section 36.11.

f_super <- p60$emp_code
f_range <- unique(out_of_range$emp_code)
f_pan <- bad_pan$emp_code
f_stranger <- unique(stranger$emp_code)
f_shared_acct <- sa_codes
f_dup <- unique(dup_salary$emp_code)
f_mobile <- employees |> filter(n() > 1, .by = mobile) |> pull(emp_code)

We also kept the employees who share a mobile number.

employees |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = mobile) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, office, cadre, mobile) |>
  arrange(mobile)

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  emp_code emp_name       office     cadre        mobile    
  <chr>    <chr>          <chr>      <chr>        <chr>     
1 009298   Saroj Agrawal  Motinagar  Clerk        6674872659
2 018163   Yogesh Agrawal Amarpur    Gauge Reader 6674872659
3 023697   Usha Nayak     Amarpur    Clerk        7717777566
4 029490   Yogesh Nayak   Dhaulagarh Clerk        7717777566
5 062156   Shobha Jain    Lakhanpur  Clerk        9812047736
6 064434   Jagdish Gupta  Lakhanpur  Clerk        9812047736
7 078349   Sanjay Singh   Lakhanpur  Clerk        9812047736


Three numbers are shared. Two are shared by a man and a woman with the same surname, most likely married couples, which is innocent. The third is the ghosts’ number.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
section: 7.9 A risk view of each employee and pensioner
text:
7.9 A risk view of each employee and pensioner
An employee caught by one test may have a good reason. One caught by several is a better use of the auditor’s time. As in Section 3.8 and Section 6.8, the simplest way to combine flags is to count them.

emp_flags <- list(
  paid_outside_service  = f_outside,
  pay_rise_no_order     = f_rise,
  two_increments        = f_twoinc,
  bank_change_arrears   = f_bank,
  arrears_twice         = f_arrears,
  above_sanctioned      = f_excess,
  no_post_in_office     = f_nopost,
  no_attendance_ever    = f_noatt_all,
  no_attendance_some    = f_noatt_some,
  past_superannuation   = f_super,
  pay_outside_range     = f_range,
  invalid_pan           = f_pan,
  not_in_master         = f_stranger,
  shared_account        = f_shared_acct,
  same_salary_twice     = f_dup,
  shared_mobile         = f_mobile
)

emp_risk <- tibble(test = names(emp_flags), emp_code = emp_flags) |>
  unnest(emp_code) |>
  distinct() |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = emp_code) |>
  left_join(payroll |> summarise(paid = sum(net_pay), .by = emp_code), by = "emp_code") |>
  mutate(office = coalesce(employees$office[match(emp_code, employees$emp_code)], "Not in master"),
         paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(emp_code, office, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

emp_risk |>
  print(n = 10)

# A tibble: 55 × 5
   emp_code office        flags paid_lakh tests                                 
   <chr>    <chr>         <int>     <dbl> <chr>                                 
 1 062156   Lakhanpur         4       4.1 above_sanctioned, no_attendance_ever,…
 2 064434   Lakhanpur         3       4.2 above_sanctioned, no_attendance_ever,…
 3 078349   Lakhanpur         3       4.1 above_sanctioned, no_attendance_ever,…
 4 099726   Kesargaon         2      12.6 no_attendance_some, past_superannuati…
 5 044813   Lakhanpur         2       6.7 above_sanctioned, shared_account      
 6 023305   Motinagar         2       2.3 paid_outside_service, no_attendance_s…
 7 091134   Amarpur           2       2.3 paid_outside_service, no_attendance_s…
 8 070815   Not in master     2       1.1 no_attendance_ever, not_in_master     
 9 014554   Head Office       1      28.1 above_sanctioned                      
10 019766   Head Office       1      23.2 above_sanctioned                      
# ℹ 45 more rows


tibble() with a list column, followed by unnest(), turns the named list into a long table. 55 of 930 employees raise at least one flag. Most raise only one. 21 of them are Lakhanpur clerks, and 7 are Assistant Engineers of the Head Office, flagged only because their office pays more people of their cadre than it has posts. The top of the list is different. The three codes with three or more flags are the three ghost clerks. Next come five codes with two flags. They are the senior clerk past 60, the real clerk whose account one ghost uses, and the clerk paid after resigning. They also include the engineer paid before joining and the person not in the master. Some serious cases, such as the arrears paid during a short-lived bank change, raise only one flag. So the count orders the work. It does not decide what to ignore.
The same idea works for pensioners.

pen_flags <- list(
  over_100_old_certificate = f_old,
  paid_on_expired_cert     = f_expired,
  family_and_service_paid  = f_both,
  commutation_twice        = f_comm,
  above_pension_rule       = f_rule,
  also_on_oap_list         = f_twolists
)

pen_risk <- tibble(test = names(pen_flags), ppo_no = pen_flags) |>
  unnest(ppo_no) |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = ppo_no) |>
  left_join(pension_paid |> summarise(paid = sum(amount), .by = ppo_no), by = "ppo_no") |>
  mutate(paid_lakh = round(paid / 1e5, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(flags), desc(paid)) |>
  select(ppo_no, flags, paid_lakh, tests)

pen_risk |>
  print(n = 6)

# A tibble: 20 × 4
  ppo_no    flags paid_lakh tests                                         
  <chr>     <int>     <dbl> <chr>                                         
1 PPO/13789     2       2.3 paid_on_expired_cert, family_and_service_paid 
2 PPO/27324     2       2   over_100_old_certificate, paid_on_expired_cert
3 PPO/16475     1      13.4 above_pension_rule                            
4 PPO/22377     1       6.6 paid_on_expired_cert                          
5 PPO/20853     1       4.4 paid_on_expired_cert                          
6 PPO/28762     1       3.7 paid_on_expired_cert                          
# ℹ 14 more rows


20 of 1,572 pensioners raise a flag. Two raise two. They are the pensioner over 100 and the pensioner whose service pension ran on after his death. A count treats every test as equal, though a pension paid after death is far more serious than a late certificate. Section 1.8 showed how to weight tests, with weights fixed before looking at the results.






NoteA flag is a lead



None of these tests proves a fraud. Each says where to look. The work that follows is ordinary audit work, with service books, registers, people and banks. The analysis tests every employee and every month, and so points that work at the right places.

7.10 Audit use case, ghost employees in one office
Let us follow the Lakhanpur clerks. We show the three codes and the real clerk, with accounts masked as in Section 9.4.

mask <- function(x) paste0("XXXXXXX", str_sub(x, -4))

employees |>
  filter(emp_code %in% c(ghost_codes, sa_real)) |>
  mutate(account = mask(bank_account)) |>
  select(emp_code, emp_name, cadre, doj, mobile, account)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  emp_code emp_name         cadre doj        mobile     account    
  <chr>    <chr>            <chr> <date>     <chr>      <chr>      
1 044813   Ram Kishore Jain Clerk 2006-01-03 7298036527 XXXXXXX8410
2 062156   Shobha Jain      Clerk 2023-03-06 9812047736 XXXXXXX8410
3 064434   Jagdish Gupta    Clerk 2022-08-01 9812047736 XXXXXXX5433
4 078349   Sanjay Singh     Clerk 2022-11-14 9812047736 XXXXXXX1259


The story fits together. The three joined between August 2022 and March 2023. They share one mobile number, which no real employee uses. One of them is paid into the account of Ram Kishore Jain, a real clerk of the same office, present in all 12 months. Not one of the three was ever marked present or on leave. Yet they were paid ₹12.5 lakh in the year, July increment included. Let us see the office month by month.

payroll |>
  filter(office == "Lakhanpur") |>
  mutate(has_attendance = paste(emp_code, month) %in% paste(attendance$emp_code, attendance$month)) |>
  summarise(paid = n_distinct(emp_code), with_attendance = sum(has_attendance), .by = month) |>
  mutate(gap = paid - with_attendance) |>
  print(n = 12)

# A tibble: 12 × 4
   month       paid with_attendance   gap
   <date>     <int>           <int> <int>
 1 2024-04-01   107             104     3
 2 2024-05-01   107             104     3
 3 2024-06-01   107             104     3
 4 2024-07-01   107             104     3
 5 2024-08-01   107             103     4
 6 2024-09-01   106             102     4
 7 2024-10-01   106             102     4
 8 2024-11-01   105             101     4
 9 2024-12-01   105             101     4
10 2025-01-01   104             101     3
11 2025-02-01   104             101     3
12 2025-03-01   104             101     3


In every month, three or more of the people Lakhanpur paid had no attendance record. In some months the gap is larger, because one other employee was on long leave. Four records agree. The payroll pays the three, the attendance system has never seen them, the posts have no room for them, and the bank details lead to one real employee. That employee, and the clerk who prepares the pay bill, are the first people to ask.

7.10.1 What the auditor does next

Ask for the service books and appointment orders of the three. Check them against the appointing authority’s own register.
Check the attendance registers and biometric records since they joined.
Hold a physical verification of every clerk of the office, on a day fixed without notice.
Ask the bank, through the department, for the holder of each account and the KYC papers.
Work out the total paid since each joined. If confirmed, the case goes to the vigilance wing for recovery, and shows that pay bills were passed with no check against attendance or posts.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
section: 7.11 Audit use case, pensions paid without a valid life certificate

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
text:
7.12 A suggested workflow


Get the full data, including the change log, attendance, sanctioned strength and life certificates. Record who extracted it and when.

Check completeness. Unique keys, every payee in the master, and totals agreeing with the bank and treasury.

Review changes in the master. Pay outside service, rises without an order, two increments, bank changes near arrears, and arrears paid twice.

Compare with the posts of each office and cadre.

Compare with attendance, after fixing the keys. Separate those never recorded from those with a run of leave.

Test the pensions. Life certificates, family and service pension together, commutation twice, the pension rule, and two lists.
Add the tests of earlier chapters.

Combine the flags for each person, and rank.

Follow up the top cases on paper and in person, and record what cleared each flag.







ImportantRemember




Payroll is usually the largest expenditure of a department, and a pension is paid for decades. A small error in the master is repeated every month.
The change log shows what the current master hides, a pay rise without an order or a bank account changed and changed back.
Count the people paid against the posts sanctioned, and against the attendance. A ghost employee leaves a salary and nothing else.
Fix the keys before a join. A code that lost its leading zeros makes every employee look absent.
The life certificate is the main control on pensions. Test every payment against it.
Many flags have innocent causes, such as leave, deputation or a late entry. Several flags on one person deserve the auditor’s time.

title: 7  Payroll and Pensions
text:
7.13 Where next
The pay bill rule book is in Chapter 31, and the rate in force in Section 16.6. Dates are in Chapter 18, lost leading zeros in Section 20.19, and shared accounts at scale in Chapter 19. Duplicates are in Chapter 34, and name matching in Chapter 35 and Chapter 36. Regression for salary is in Section 40.9, and personal data in Chapter 9. The ledger and the bank are tested in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2, and vendors in Chapter 6. Chapter 8, next, turns to revenue and tax.

A wider window for bank changes. Find the arrears bills paid within 60 days after a change of bank account, instead of 15. How many are there, and are any new ones suspicious?

title: 8  Revenue and Tax
text:
8.1 Where revenue leaks
A State taxes the supply of goods and services. About two thousand dealers in eight districts file a return every month. Each return declares the dealer’s sales, the tax due on them, and the credit claimed for tax already paid on purchases. The dealer pays the rest. Nobody checks most returns in detail. So a dealer may declare less than was sold, charge an old lower rate, or claim a refund that is not due. A dealer may stop filing and carry on trading. A shell firm may exist only to pass on credit.
Most chapters of this part look for money wrongly spent. Revenue audit looks for money not collected. It asks two questions. Was all the tax that should have been assessed actually assessed and collected? Were exemptions, concessions and refunds allowed correctly? The loss is harder to see, because nothing was paid out. It shows only when the return is read against another record, such as the movement of goods, the buyer’s own return or the guideline value of a property.
Earlier chapters already hold several revenue tests, such as the credit reconciliation of Section 2.5, circular trading in Section 55.4, and refund models in Chapter 41. This chapter runs them together for one department, in a few lines each, and adds what the book lacks. These are tests of registration and filing, of tax declared against third-party data, and of rates, thresholds and refunds. Others look for shell dealers, check stamp duty on property, and age the demands not collected. It then combines the flags for each dealer, and follows two cases to the end.
A flag is not a finding. Many flags in tax data have an innocent cause, such as a seasonal trade, an export or a genuine closure. The aim is to find the few that need a question.
Prerequisites
A tax on supplies rests on a few records. Each can be read against the others.
The controls are simple. Every registered dealer should file every return. What a dealer declares should agree with what third parties record. Tax should be charged at the rate in force on the date of supply. A concession or a refund should go only to those entitled to it. A demand should be collected before the time to recover it runs out.

title: 8  Revenue and Tax
section: 8.2 Our data, a year of a State tax on goods and services
text:
8.2 Our data, a year of a State tax on goods and services
Our auditee is the tax department of an imaginary State, with eight districts. We have its records for 2024-25. All names and numbers are made up. There are twelve tables.


dealers is the registration master. It holds the dealer ID, name, a PAN-like code, trade, district, address, dates of registration and cancellation, scheme, bank account and mobile.

returns has one row per dealer per month filed. It holds turnover, exports, exempt sales, taxable value at 5%, 12% and 18%, output tax, input tax credit (ITC) claimed, tax paid and the filing date.

movement summarises the movement records of goods sent by each dealer each month.

buyer_reports holds the purchases each buyer reported from each supplier each month.

treasury holds the tax credited to the State’s account, by return month.

rate_master gives the rate for each commodity code from each date. supply_lines holds the invoices of forty dealers of building material, with the rate charged.

refunds holds the refund claims, with dates, amounts and the bank account credited.

demands holds the tax demands raised after scrutiny, back to 2017, and collections the amounts recovered.

deeds holds about three thousand property documents registered in one sub-registrar office, and guideline the guideline rate per square metre for each locality and type of property.

The tax follows a few example norms. Most goods are taxed at 5%, 12% or 18%. A retailer with a yearly turnover up to ₹1.5 crore may choose a composition scheme, paying a flat 1% of turnover with no credit. In our example the scheme is closed to dealers of iron and steel and of electronics. A return is due by the 20th of the next month. The rate on ceramic tiles rose from 12% to 18% on 1 October 2024. Stamp duty is 6% of the declared value or the guideline value, whichever is higher. A demand must be recovered within five years of being raised. These are illustrative rules for this example only. In real work, apply the actual law, rates and time limits of your own jurisdiction.
Most of the data is routine. Fertiliser sales rise and fall with the sowing seasons, and some small fertiliser dealers sell nothing in winter. Some dealers closed during the year and had their registrations cancelled. A few dealers are dormant and file nil returns. Some exporters receive large refunds of credit, as the law intends. Some property documents valued below the guideline value were referred for valuation, as the rules allow. Into this, these cases have been planted.


Nil returns while goods move. A steel wholesaler files nil returns from September while its goods keep moving.

Turnover hidden. An electronics wholesaler declares about a third of its sales, in round lakh, while its buyers report far more.

A sharp fall. A cement dealer’s tax falls sharply from October while the trade grows.

An old rate. A building material dealer keeps charging 12% on tiles after the rate rose to 18%.

Bunching. Two dozen retailers keep their turnover just under the composition limit, and three dealers in excluded trades use the scheme.

Refunds to new linked dealers. Three “exporters” registered in November share a bank account and a mobile, and receive refunds within days.

A refund above all tax paid. A dealer registered in August is refunded more than all the tax it ever paid.

A ring of shell dealers. Four dealers registered in June trade goods round in a circle, and stop filing after January.

Stamp duty. Documents in one locality are valued far below the guideline value. One property is sold twice by the same seller. Shops are registered as houses.

Old demands. Large demands of 2020-21 are uncollected and close to the time limit.

Let us build the data.

Code to create the tax department’s dataset.seed(2526)

fy_start  <- as.Date("2024-04-01")
fy_end    <- as.Date("2025-03-31")
fy_months <- seq(fy_start, by = "month", length.out = 12)
month_end <- function(m) ceiling_date(m, "month") - 1

districts <- c("Dhanpur", "Kesarganj", "Chandgarh", "Sonpur", "Rampura", "Lakhanpur", "Bhimgarh", "Navgaon")
trades <- tribble(
  ~trade,              ~main_rate, ~moves, ~share, ~exempt,
  "Iron and steel",    18,         TRUE,   0.11,   0,
  "Cement",            18,         TRUE,   0.08,   0,
  "Building material", 18,         TRUE,   0.10,   0,
  "Textiles",           5,         TRUE,   0.12,   0,
  "Electronics",       18,         TRUE,   0.10,   0,
  "Grocery",            5,         TRUE,   0.17,   0.35,
  "Fertiliser",         5,         TRUE,   0.07,   0,
  "Pharmaceuticals",   12,         TRUE,   0.08,   0,
  "Restaurants",        5,         FALSE,  0.11,   0,
  "Scrap and metals",  18,         TRUE,   0.06,   0)
season_flat <- c(0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 1.00, 1.08, 1.10, 1.00, 0.97, 0.95, 1.15)
season_fert <- c(0.55, 0.85, 1.70, 1.75, 1.05, 0.75, 1.55, 1.45, 0.85, 0.60, 0.50, 0.50)

# ---- Names and identifiers ----
pre <- c("Shree", "Jai", "New", "Maa", "Om", "Sai", "Shiv", "Ganpati", "Balaji", "Laxmi", "Krishna",
         "Durga", "Gayatri", "Vinayak", "Radhe", "Bharat", "Navyug", "Pragati", "Surya", "Kamdhenu",
         "Annapurna", "Hanuman", "Mahavir", "Ambika", "Shubham", "Ashirwad", "Gurukripa", "Sagar",
         "Tirupati", "Vaibhav", "Kailash", "Uday", "Saraswati", "Rajdhani", "Prakash", "Moti")
suffix <- list(
  "Iron and steel" = c("Steels", "Iron Traders", "Steel Corporation", "Iron Stores"),
  "Cement" = c("Cement Agency", "Cement Depot", "Cement Traders"),
  "Building material" = c("Tiles and Sanitary", "Building Materials", "Hardware Stores", "Ceramics"),
  "Textiles" = c("Textiles", "Cloth Stores", "Fabrics", "Saree Centre"),
  "Electronics" = c("Electronics", "Electricals", "Digital World", "Mobile Point"),
  "Grocery" = c("Kirana Stores", "Provision Stores", "Traders", "General Stores"),
  "Fertiliser" = c("Krishi Kendra", "Fertilisers", "Khad Bhandar", "Agro Agency"),
  "Pharmaceuticals" = c("Medical Agency", "Pharma", "Medicos", "Drug House"),
  "Restaurants" = c("Restaurant", "Bhojnalaya", "Dhaba", "Sweets and Restaurant"),
  "Scrap and metals" = c("Metals", "Scrap Traders", "Alloys", "Metal Udyog"))
streets <- c("Station Road", "Sadar Bazaar", "Gandhi Chowk", "Mandi Road", "Civil Lines", "Industrial Area",
             "Transport Nagar", "Main Market", "Subhash Marg", "Tilak Path", "Old City", "Bus Stand Road",
             "Nehru Market", "Ring Road", "Kachehri Road", "Ganj Bazaar", "Hospital Road", "Railway Colony")
make_pan    <- function(n) paste0(replicate(n, paste(sample(LETTERS, 3, TRUE), collapse = "")),
                                  sample(c("F", "P"), n, TRUE), sample(LETTERS, n, TRUE),
                                  sprintf("%04d", sample(1:9999, n, TRUE)), sample(LETTERS, n, TRUE))
make_acct   <- function(n) sprintf("%012.0f", runif(n, 1e11, 9.99e11))
make_mobile <- function(n) paste0(sample(6:9, n, TRUE), sprintf("%09.0f", runif(n, 1e8, 9.99e8)))
pick_one    <- function(x, n = 1) x[sample.int(length(x), n)]

# ---- Registration master ----
nd <- 1990
d <- tibble(trade = sample(trades$trade, nd, TRUE, prob = trades$share),
            district = sample(districts, nd, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(tier = if_else(trade == "Restaurants", "Retailer",
                        sample(c("Manufacturer", "Wholesaler", "Retailer"), nd, TRUE, prob = c(0.07, 0.26, 0.67))),
         annual_lakh = case_when(tier == "Manufacturer" ~ rlnorm(nd, log(1400), 0.8),
                                 tier == "Wholesaler"   ~ rlnorm(nd, log(380), 0.7),
                                 TRUE                   ~ rlnorm(nd, log(85), 0.75)),
         reg_date = fy_start - sample(60:4200, nd, TRUE),
         cancel_date = as.Date(NA),
         exporter = FALSE)
new_reg <- sample(nd, 110)
d$reg_date[new_reg] <- fy_start + sample(5:320, 110, TRUE)
# Genuine closures, cancelled during the year
closed <- sample(setdiff(seq_len(nd), new_reg), 24)
d$cancel_date[closed] <- fy_start + sample(40:300, 24, TRUE)
# Genuine exporters, and one registered in May 2024
exp_i <- pick_one(which(d$tier != "Retailer" & d$trade %in% c("Textiles", "Pharmaceuticals", "Electronics") &
                          !seq_len(nd) %in% c(new_reg, closed)), 24)
d$exporter[exp_i] <- TRUE
new_exp <- pick_one(which(d$tier == "Wholesaler" & d$trade == "Textiles" & !d$exporter &
                            !seq_len(nd) %in% c(new_reg, closed)))
d$exporter[new_exp] <- TRUE
d$reg_date[new_exp] <- as.Date("2024-05-14")
d$annual_lakh[new_exp] <- 600
# Composition scheme, example norm: retailers up to Rs 1.5 crore, not open to two trades
excluded_trades <- c("Iron and steel", "Electronics")
d <- d |>
  mutate(scheme = if_else(tier == "Retailer" & annual_lakh < 150 & !trade %in% excluded_trades &
                            runif(nd) < 0.55, "Composition", "Regular"))
used <- c(new_reg, closed, exp_i, new_exp)
old <- d$reg_date < fy_start & is.na(d$cancel_date) & !d$exporter
pick <- function(cond, n = 1) {
  i <- pick_one(setdiff(which(cond), used), n)
  used <<- c(used, i)
  i
}
# Planted. Twenty-four retailers keep their turnover just under the composition limit
bunch_i <- pick(old & d$tier == "Retailer" & d$scheme == "Regular" &
                  !d$trade %in% c(excluded_trades, "Restaurants") & d$annual_lakh > 160 & d$annual_lakh < 300, 24)
d$scheme[bunch_i] <- "Composition"
d$annual_lakh[bunch_i] <- runif(24, 145.5, 149.8)
# Planted. Composition taken in trades not eligible for it
inelig_i <- pick(old & d$tier == "Retailer" & d$trade %in% excluded_trades & d$annual_lakh < 110, 3)
d$scheme[inelig_i] <- "Composition"
reg_old <- old & d$scheme == "Regular"
# Planted. Nil returns from September while goods keep moving
p_nil  <- pick(reg_old & d$tier == "Wholesaler" & d$trade == "Iron and steel")
# Planted. Declares about a third of the turnover, in round lakh
p_hide <- pick(reg_old & d$tier == "Wholesaler" & d$trade == "Electronics" & d$district == "Dhanpur")
d$annual_lakh[p_hide] <- 720
# Planted. Tax falls sharply from October while the trade grows
p_drop <- pick(reg_old & d$tier == "Wholesaler" & d$trade == "Cement" & d$district == "Kesarganj")
d$annual_lakh[p_drop] <- 560
# Planted. Keeps charging the old rate on tiles after the rise
p_rate <- pick(reg_old & d$tier == "Wholesaler" & d$trade == "Building material")
d$annual_lakh[p_rate] <- 450
# Planted. Twelve dealers stop filing, three of them still moving goods
stop_i <- pick(reg_old & d$tier != "Manufacturer" & d$trade != "Restaurants", 12)
stop_after <- sample(fy_months[4:8], 12, TRUE)
